settings.language.title: Language
settings.language.desc: The language OpsMaxx uses. Anything not translated yet stays in English.
onboarding.questions.containers.question: Do you work with containers?
onboarding.questions.containers.detail: Docker and Kubernetes panels on every server.
onboarding.questions.containers.cost: Reads only, and nothing runs until you open the panel.
onboarding.questions.fleet.question: Do you look after a fleet, or a couple of machines?
onboarding.questions.fleet.detail: Inventory, drift, a change log and security posture across the workspace.
onboarding.questions.fleet.cost: These read every host on a schedule, including running its package manager once an hour.
onboarding.questions.operate.question: Do you change servers from here, or only watch them?
onboarding.questions.operate.detail: Run commands across many servers, apply package updates, leave jobs running.
onboarding.questions.operate.cost: This is the half of the app that writes to your servers.
onboarding.questions.cicd.question: Do your servers get changed by a pipeline?
onboarding.questions.cicd.detail: Jenkins, GitLab CI or GitHub Actions, beside the server the run changed.
onboarding.questions.cicd.cost: This one talks to a service outside your estate, on a timer, with a token you paste in.
onboarding.prefs.updates.label: Updates & releases
onboarding.prefs.updates.detail: How OpsMaxx finds and takes new versions. Everything here is also in Settings › General.
onboarding.prefs.updateChannel.label: Which builds to be offered
onboarding.prefs.updateChannel.detail: Beta cascades — a beta user is offered betas and stable releases, whichever is newer.
onboarding.prefs.updateAutoCheck.label: Check automatically
onboarding.prefs.updateAutoCheck.detail: Off means OpsMaxx only ever looks when you press the button.
onboarding.prefs.updateCheckIntervalHour: Zero means only at launch; anything else is additionally re-checked while open.
onboarding.prefs.updateAutoDownload.deta: Nothing installs itself either way — applying an update is always a separate press.
onboarding.prefs.fleet.label: Watching the estate
onboarding.prefs.fleet.detail: Whether OpsMaxx samples your servers when nobody is looking at them. Off by default, and this is the switch worth understanding before you leave it.
onboarding.prefs.fleetSamplingEnabled.de: On means OpsMaxx keeps connections to every server in the workspace open on a schedule, whether or not the monitor is on screen — so alerts and capacity trends keep working while the window is closed. Off means a server is only measured while you are looking at it.
onboarding.prefs.fleetSamplingIntervalMs: Every sample is one connection per server. More often is not more accurate.
onboarding.prefs.alerts.label: Alerts
onboarding.prefs.alerts.detail: The master switch for every alert and every webhook: CPU and memory over the threshold, full disks, failed systemd units, load average.
onboarding.prefs.resourceAlertsEnabled.l: Tell me when a server is struggling
onboarding.prefs.resourceAlertsEnabled.d: Covers failed units and full disks as well as CPU and memory. Switching it off also takes down any alerts already showing.
The same figure applies to CPU and to memory. Disk has its own, fixed at 85%. Per-server overrides live in Settings.
onboarding.prefs.look.label: Look & feel
onboarding.prefs.look.detail: Both of these are instant and both are in Settings › Appearance afterwards.
onboarding.prefs.theme.label: Theme
onboarding.prefs.theme.detail: System follows your operating system, including when it changes at sunset.
onboarding.prefs.compactDensity.label: Density
onboarding.prefs.compactDensity.detail: Compact tightens row heights and padding across every table in the app.
onboarding.personas.devops.label: DevOps engineer
onboarding.personas.devops.detail: Containers and pipelines, and you change the servers as well as watching them.
onboarding.personas.cloud.label: Cloud / platform engineer
onboarding.personas.cloud.detail: Mostly Kubernetes, with an eye on what the estate is made of and where it is heading.
onboarding.personas.infra.label: Infrastructure / sysadmin
onboarding.personas.infra.detail: You own the machines: what is on them, what needs patching, who can get in.
onboarding.personas.sre.label: SRE / on-call
onboarding.personas.sre.detail: You need to know something is wrong before somebody tells you. Mostly reading.
onboarding.setup.persona.title: What do you do?
onboarding.setup.persona.intro: Optional — it answers the next four questions for you, and every one stays editable. Nothing you choose here is permanent.
onboarding.setup.review.title: Ready when you are
onboarding.setup.review.intro: Click any answer to go back and change it.
onboarding.setup.review.prefsHint: Sensible defaults; open one to change it.
onboarding.setup.hint.text: {{counts}}. Anything not listed here — revoking keys, unattended rules, reading other accounts’ access — stays off and lives in Settings.
onboarding.tour.connections.title: Start with a server
onboarding.tour.connections.body: Add a server once and reuse it everywhere — terminal, files, monitoring, tunnels and databases all work off the same connection. Each can route through unlimited jump hosts, each with its own credentials. If you already keep hosts in ~/.ssh/config, import them instead of retyping; ProxyJump comes across too.
onboarding.tour.connections.action: Add a server, or import your SSH config.
onboarding.tour.done.title: Everything else is behind one shortcut
onboarding.tour.done.body: Cmd/Ctrl+K opens the command palette, which reaches every server, workspace, tunnel and action in the app. The rest of OpsMaxx introduces itself as you open it, and this walkthrough is in Settings if you want it again.
onboarding.tips.dismissTitle: Got it — do not show this again
onboarding.tips.workspaces.title: Workspaces keep clients and environments apart
onboarding.tips.workspaces.body: Servers, databases, tunnels and vault entries each belong to a workspace — switch with the picker in the title bar, and password-protect a workspace to keep one client’s infrastructure out of sight. A vault entry can also be marked shared, when the same credential is genuinely used from several workspaces.
onboarding.tips.workspaces.action: Try the workspace picker at the top left.
onboarding.tips.vault.title: The vault is where credentials live
onboarding.tips.vault.body: Passwords, SSH keys and API keys, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a master password. Entries belong to a workspace, or are marked shared when the same credential is used from several. A server references an entry rather than keeping its own copy, so rotating a credential is one edit instead of a hunt. On a Mac with Touch ID you can unlock with a fingerprint.
onboarding.tips.monitor.title: Monitoring, including what is broken
onboarding.tips.monitor.body: Live CPU, memory, disk and network per server, totalled across the fleet. Failed systemd units and listening ports come back on the same poll, so you can see what a server exposes and what has fallen over without opening a shell.
onboarding.tips.tunnels.title: Tunnels, and databases behind a bastion
onboarding.tips.tunnels.body: Local and remote port forwards plus a SOCKS5 proxy. The database client speaks PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB and Redis, and can reach a database that is only routable from inside the network.
onboarding.tips.databases.title: Databases, over a connection you already have
onboarding.tips.databases.body: Five engines, with the query editor and schema browser reading through an SSH tunnel or a VPN profile when the database is not routable from here. Credentials go to your operating system’s secure storage, never into the workspace file.
onboarding.tips.ai.title: AI agents, without handing over credentials
onboarding.tips.ai.body: Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Codex can run commands and read files through OpsMaxx, but never see a password, key, hostname or username. You choose per capability what is allowed, asked about or refused, and every action lands in the audit log.
onboarding.tips.docker.title: Containers, on whichever server they are on
onboarding.tips.docker.body: Every container on a server with its logs and a shell inside it, grouped by compose project, using the docker binary already there. The disk view itemises what is reclaimable and removes only what you tick — nothing is pruned wholesale. A shell inside a container is arbitrary code execution on that host, which is the same power the terminal tab already grants on the same credential.
onboarding.tips.kubernetes.title: Clusters, read through the kubectl already on the server
onboarding.tips.kubernetes.body: Contexts, namespaces, pods and their logs, plus nodes, workloads and what is actually requesting your capacity. Reading only: it never switches your context, never execs into a pod, and never applies or deletes anything — so there is nothing here that can change a cluster.
onboarding.tips.cicd.title: Pipelines, beside the servers they change
onboarding.tips.cicd.body: Connect Jenkins, GitLab CI or GitHub Actions and read what it did — run history and the log of the step that failed — next to the server the run changed. This is the one tab that talks to a service outside your estate, on a timer, with a token you paste in. Starting and cancelling are here too, behind a second module you switch on separately.
onboarding.tips.processes.title: Long-lived programs on this machine
onboarding.tips.processes.body: A dev server, a worker, a script that should outlive the terminal that started it — with restart policies, backoff, crash-loop detection and a log ring, from the supervisor that already keeps VPN engines alive. Nothing here runs on a remote server and nothing starts by itself: the only thing that starts a process is you pressing Start.
settings.credProxy.token.created: Token for “{{name}}” created and copied. It is the only copy you need — OpsMaxx keeps it too.
settings.credProxy.token.unreadable: That token’s value could not be read.
settings.credProxy.token.revokeConfirm:
Revoke “{{name}}”?

Anything still using this token starts being refused immediately, and it cannot be un-revoked. Other tokens are unaffected.
settings.credProxy.entryMissing: a vault entry that is no longer there
settings.credProxy.title: API credential proxy
settings.credProxy.descIntro: A script, a dev server or an agent calls a third-party API through OpsMaxx without ever holding the key. Point its base URL at the address below; the credential is added here, on the way out, and never comes back in a response.
settings.credProxy.descOptIn: Nothing is intercepted and no certificate is installed — a caller opts in by pointing at us, which is why an unconfigured tool is unaffected.
settings.credProxy.port.title: Port
settings.credProxy.parked.vaultLocked_on: The vault is locked, so {{count}} call was parked since {{time}} rather than sent without a credential.
settings.credProxy.parked.vaultLocked_ot: The vault is locked, so {{count}} calls were parked since {{time}} rather than sent without a credential.
settings.credProxy.parked.unlockReason: Unlocking releases the calls parked while the vault was closed.
settings.credProxy.parked.entryEmpty_one: A rule points at a vault entry that no longer holds anything. {{count}} call refused since {{time}}.
settings.credProxy.parked.entryEmpty_oth: A rule points at a vault entry that no longer holds anything. {{count}} calls refused since {{time}}.
settings.credProxy.tokens.title: Tokens
settings.credProxy.tokens.header: One per caller, sent as {{header}} on every request.
settings.credProxy.tokens.perCaller: Give each script or agent its own, so revoking one does not stop the others.
settings.credProxy.tokens.expiryTitle: Optional end date. A token with no end date never expires.
settings.credProxy.tokens.none: No tokens, so every request is refused. Create one above and give it to the script that needs it.
settings.credProxy.rules.title: Rules
settings.credProxy.rules.desc: One destination, one credential, one way of sending it. Nothing applies by default: a destination with no rule is refused, never forwarded.
settings.credProxy.rules.unavailable: This build does not expose the credential proxy, so what it would allow cannot be read here.
settings.credProxy.rules.none: No rules yet, so the proxy will refuse everything. That is the safe state, not a broken one.
settings.credProxy.draft.originHint: The exact origin, and only that origin. A rule for api.example.com does not cover api.example.com.something-else, and it does not follow a redirect anywhere either.
settings.credProxy.calls.title: Recent calls
settings.credProxy.calls.desc: Destination, rule, outcome and how long it took. Never the body, the headers or the query string — a rule that puts the key in a query parameter is exactly the rule whose query string must not be written down.
settings.webhooks.testIgnoresOne: {{delivered}} Nothing else will be sent, though — the test ignores the switches, and {{a}} is off.
settings.webhooks.testIgnoresBoth: {{delivered}} Nothing else will be sent, though — the test ignores the switches, and {{a}} and {{b}} are off.
settings.webhooks.title: Send alerts to a webhook
settings.webhooks.desc: POSTs a small JSON message to any HTTPS endpoint — Slack, Discord, Teams and most alerting systems accept one. Only the server’s name, what fired and when are sent; never a server, an IP, a log line or command output.
settings.webhooks.addUrlHint: Add a URL below to enable this.
settings.webhooks.dependsOnAlerts: It carries what Alerts raises, so that switch has to be on too. And nothing is raised while you are elsewhere unless servers are checked in the background — so with that off, this stays silent in exactly the case you set it up for.
settings.webhooks.url.title: Webhook URL
settings.webhooks.url.saved: A URL is saved. It is stored with your other secrets and is never shown again — paste a new one to replace it, or save an empty field to remove it.
settings.webhooks.url.notSaved: Stored with your other secrets, not in settings or backups. https only, since the URL is itself a credential.
settings.webhooks.test.title: Test delivery
settings.webhooks.test.desc: Sends one sample alert now, so a wrong URL is found here rather than during an incident.
settings.webhooks.resolved.title: Also send when it recovers
settings.webhooks.resolved.desc: An alert with no resolution leaves the reader working out whether it is still happening.
settings.webhooks.delivery.dropped_one: {{count}} alert dropped since launch. More than 30 in one minute are discarded rather than queued, so those were never delivered.
settings.webhooks.delivery.dropped_other: {{count}} alerts dropped since launch. More than 30 in one minute are discarded rather than queued, so those were never delivered.
settings.webhooks.delivery.none: No alert has been delivered since launch.

settings.shortcuts.emptyExport: That export has no shortcuts in it, so nothing was changed.
settings.shortcuts.imported_one: Imported {{count}} shortcut. Anything not in the file is back to its default.
settings.shortcuts.imported_other: Imported {{count}} shortcuts. Anything not in the file is back to its default.
settings.shortcuts.hint: Click a shortcut and press the keys you want. Backspace clears it, Esc cancels.
settings.shortcuts.resetDone: Every shortcut is back to its default.
settings.shortcuts.replacesInHttp: In the HTTP client this replaces {{names}}
settings.shortcuts.shadowedInHttp: Shadowed in the HTTP client by {{name}}
settings.shortcuts.conflictGoTo: {{name}} uses the same keys — go to it
settings.machineGrants.grantedUndated: Granted before OpsMaxx recorded grant dates
settings.machineGrants.revoked: Revoked. This machine can no longer read that secret on its own.
settings.machineGrants.unavailableTitle: Grants cannot be listed right now
settings.machineGrants.unavailableMessag: The preload bridge on this build has no way to read them. Restart the app; if it persists, this version cannot show them and nothing can be revoked from here.
settings.machineGrants.emptyTitle: Nothing runs without your master password
settings.machineGrants.emptyMessage: No secret on this machine is readable without it. Scheduled backups and addy will ask you to unlock after a restart.
settings.machineGrants.orphaned: Orphaned — this authorises something that no longer exists.
settings.sshSessions.keep.title: Keep authenticated connection
settings.sshSessions.keep.desc: New sessions, file browsing and monitoring reuse an existing authenticated connection instead of logging in again. On servers with two-factor authentication, a code is only requested when no connection is being reused — so this sets how often you are asked.
settings.sshSessions.shared.title: Shared connections
settings.sshSessions.shared.some: Disconnecting one forces the next connection to that server to authenticate again.
settings.sshSessions.shared.none: None open. The first connection to a server authenticates and is then reused.
settings.sshSessions.disconnected: Disconnected {{target}}. The next connection to it will authenticate again.
settings.alertCoverage.running: Background checks are running, so alerts fire wherever you are in the app.
settings.alertCoverage.requestedNotRunni: Background checks are switched on but not running right now — see the reason below. Until they are, a server is only sampled while its monitor is on screen.
settings.alertCoverage.foregroundOnly: Without background checks below, a server is only sampled while its monitor is on screen — so an alert can only fire while you are already looking at it.
settings.alertCoverage.appRoot: Job failures and tunnels are watched from the moment the app starts, whether or not background checks are on: a job reports its own steps, and tunnels are polled every ten seconds.
settings.alertCoverage.readOnDemand: Database verdicts are the exception, and it is not a small one: they exist only because somebody opened the Databases page and read it. Nothing produces them in the background, so a database that goes into alarm overnight is not noticed until it is next read.
settings.alertCoverage.postureSweep: OOM kills and certificate expiry are read by the security posture probe, about once an hour. It has TWO switches, not one: it runs on the background sweep above, and only while the Security posture module is on for this workspace. With either of those off nothing reads them at all — not even while a monitor is on screen — until somebody presses Check now on the Security posture panel. With both on they are read about once an hour and raise with no screen open.
settings.retention.contactedSeconds_one: Background checking is on, so every server in this workspace is contacted every second.
settings.retention.contactedSeconds_othe: Background checking is on, so every server in this workspace is contacted every {{count}} seconds.
settings.retention.contactedMinutes_one: Background checking is on, so every server in this workspace is contacted every minute.
settings.retention.contactedMinutes_othe: Background checking is on, so every server in this workspace is contacted every {{count}} minutes.
settings.retention.overrideNotice: Their connection never sits idle long enough for this to expire, so it does not apply to them at any setting — including Immediately. On a server with two-factor authentication, no new code is requested while OpsMaxx is running.
settings.backupPanel.error.exportFailed: Nothing was written: {{error}} Your passphrase is still in the fields above.
settings.backupPanel.error.exportFallbac: the file could not be saved.
settings.backupPanel.error.fileDidNotOpe: {{file}} did not open. {{error}} The passphrase is the one chosen when that backup was made — not your vault master password.
settings.backupPanel.error.restoreFallba: The restore could not be completed.
settings.backupPanel.error.deletePartial: The rest was deleted, but some of it is still there. {{error}} Run it again to finish, or restore the backup above.
settings.backupPanel.error.deleteFallbac: A file could not be removed.
settings.backupPanel.status.dirtyDesc: Your connections have changed since the last export. Download a new backup and store it somewhere safe so this configuration can be recovered — or set up a destination below to have one written on a schedule.
settings.backupPanel.download.heading: Download backup
settings.backupPanel.download.desc: Writes a single encrypted file containing your workspaces, servers, databases, tunnels, stored credentials, vault and trusted host keys. Credentials are re-encrypted under this passphrase, so the file restores on any machine — and is unreadable without it.
settings.backupPanel.download.readyTitle: Choose where to save the backup
settings.backupPanel.download.tooShortTi: Pick a passphrase of at least {{min}} characters first
settings.backupPanel.download.passphrase: Choose a passphrase you can find again — there is no way to open the file without it, and nothing here can reset it.
settings.backupPanel.restore.heading: Restore from backup
settings.backupPanel.restore.desc: Replaces everything currently in this app with the contents of the backup file. Type the passphrase for that backup first, then choose the file — you get to see what is inside it before anything is replaced, and the app restarts once the restore completes. The recorded history of the servers already on this machine is cleared as part of the restore: a backup does not carry history, and keeping the old estate's would leave two estates in one timeline.
settings.backupPanel.restore.chooseTitle: Pick the backup file to read
settings.backupPanel.staged.title: Replace current data?
settings.backupPanel.danger.heading: Danger zone
settings.backupPanel.danger.desc: Permanently deletes every workspace, server, database, tunnel, stored credential, the vault, trusted host keys and AI/MCP configuration — everything a backup covers, gone from this machine. It also deletes the recorded history: every sample, event and observed fact about your servers. This cannot be undone from within the app, and a backup does not contain the history — only what a backup covers can be brought back.
settings.backupPanel.danger.backUpFirstD: Your data has changed since the last backup — download one before deleting anything, or whatever changed since then is gone for good.
settings.backupPanel.danger.confirmTitle: This deletes everything on this machine
settings.backupPanel.danger.confirmDesc: Type {{word}} to confirm. The app restarts once it's done.
settings.backupDest.heading: Backup destinations
settings.backupDest.intro: Somewhere for a backup to go that is not this machine, written on a schedule and checked after every write. Each generation is read back off the destination and decrypted before the run is called a success, and older generations are only deleted once the new one has passed both.
settings.backupDest.exposure.title: A backup is your whole vault, wherever you send it
settings.backupDest.exposure.desc: Every file written here contains your stored credentials, your vault and your trusted host keys, encrypted under one passphrase. Choosing a destination is choosing somewhere for those to live.
settings.backupDest.corrupt.title: Your destinations could not be read
settings.backupDest.corrupt.desc: {{reason}} Saving a destination from here moves the unreadable file aside rather than writing over it, so what was in it stays recoverable by hand.
settings.backupDest.empty.title: No destinations yet
settings.backupDest.empty.message: Backups still work through the file you download above; a destination is what makes them happen on a schedule and get checked afterwards.
settings.backupDest.status.testRestored: {{name}} — read back off the destination and test-restored
settings.backupDest.status.matched: {{name}} — read back off the destination and matched
settings.backupDest.status.testRestoredR: {{name}} — read back off the destination and test-restored, {{count}} older removed
settings.backupDest.status.matchedRemove: {{name}} — read back off the destination and matched, {{count}} older removed
settings.backupDest.card.title: {{name}} · {{kind}}
settings.backupDest.card.missingServer: a server that no longer exists
settings.backupDest.card.addyLocation: the relay this device is enrolled on
settings.backupDest.card.needPassphraseT: Type the passphrase to encrypt this backup with
settings.backupDest.card.backUpNowTitle: Write a backup here now and verify it
settings.backupDest.card.removeTitle: Removes this destination from OpsMaxx. The backups already at it are left alone.
settings.backupDest.dump.note: A dump is plain SQL, written alongside the backups and encrypted by nothing. Retention does not touch it, and a restore cannot read it — it is for the database, not for this app.
settings.backupDest.dump.fallback: the dump could not be taken.
settings.backupDest.browse.unreadable: That destination could not be read.
settings.backupDest.browse.empty: No OpsMaxx backups at this destination yet.
settings.backupDest.browse.openTitle: Download it and show what is inside before anything is replaced
settings.backupDest.browse.needPassphras: Type the passphrase used for that backup first
settings.backupDest.editor.machineRefuse: This machine would not store the passphrase.
settings.backupDest.editor.sftpNote: Uploads over that server's existing credentials — this destination stores none of its own, and an unattended run refuses an unknown host key rather than asking.
settings.backupDest.editor.addyNote:
Writes to the relay this device is already enrolled on. There is nothing to configure and no credential to store: it authenticates with this device's own key, and the relay address and account come from the enrolment.
The bundle is encrypted with the passphrase like every other destination, and sealed a second time under your account key on the way out — so the relay holds something it cannot read even if the passphrase leaks.
settings.backupDest.editor.accessKeyEntr: Vault entry holding the access key…
settings.backupDest.editor.accessKeyNote: The access key id goes in that entry's username and the secret key in its secret. It has to be a vault entry: application settings travel inside every backup written here, so a secret key kept there would be sitting in the bucket it unlocks.
settings.backupDest.editor.unlockReason: Unlocking lets you choose the vault entry holding this bucket's keys.
settings.backupDest.editor.passphraseEnt: Vault entry holding the backup passphrase…
settings.backupDest.editor.vaultNote: Nobody is present at 3am to type a passphrase, so a scheduled run reads one from the vault. The vault keeps resolving after the idle timeout, so this survives a screen left alone — but not a restart, until somebody unlocks. A run skipped for that reason says so in the status bar rather than quietly not happening.
settings.backupDest.editor.machineStored: Stored on this machine — type to replace
settings.backupDest.editor.machineNote: Kept in this machine’s keychain, so runs continue after a restart with nobody present. It is deliberately left out of every backup — a passphrase inside the file it protects would protect nothing — which means restoring onto another machine does not bring it back. Write it down somewhere a lost laptop does not take with it. Anyone with this machine can open every generation this destination has written.
settings.updatePanel.heading: About & Updates
settings.updatePanel.noSelfInstall.mac: macOS builds here are not notarized, so OpsMaxx cannot safely replace itself automatically — download the new version and open it the same way as the first install.
settings.updatePanel.noSelfInstall.porta: This is the portable build, which runs from wherever you put it — OpsMaxx cannot replace its own executable, so download the new version and swap it in.
settings.updatePanel.noSelfInstall.other: This build cannot install updates itself — download the new version from the releases page.
settings.updatePanel.ready.title: Update ready
settings.updatePanel.ready.willRestart: OpsMaxx will restart to finish installing v{{version}}.
settings.updatePanel.ready.cannotInstall: v{{version}} has been downloaded, but this build cannot install it itself.
settings.updatePanel.manual.title: v{{version}} is available
settings.updatePanel.error.title: Update check failed
settings.updatePanel.error.desc: {{message}} — you can always grab the latest release directly.
settings.updatePanel.channel.heading: Update channel
settings.updatePanel.channel.title: Channel
settings.updatePanel.channel.desc: Stable is the released build. Beta gets new features earlier, and gets their bugs earlier too — it is the build that has not been through as many hands yet.
settings.updatePanel.auto.heading: Automatic updates
settings.updatePanel.auto.checkDesc: Off means OpsMaxx only looks when you press Check for updates.
settings.updatePanel.auto.intervalDesc: Every check happens at launch as well. A longer interval only affects an app that stays open for days.
settings.updatePanel.auto.downloadDesc: Fetch the update in the background as soon as one is found. Off means you are told first and press Download yourself.
settings.updatePanel.auto.installDesc: Apply a downloaded update the next time you close OpsMaxx, instead of waiting for you to restart it now.
settings.updatePanel.auto.installUnknown: Unavailable until OpsMaxx knows what this build can install.
settings.updatePanel.ignore.ignoringDesc: The status bar stays quiet about this version. A newer one brings the indicator back on its own.
settings.updatePanel.ignore.desc: Hide the status-bar indicator for v{{version}}. Updates stay on, and the next version will say so.
settings.updatePanel.restartModal.title: Restart to finish updating?
settings.updatePanel.restartModal.subtit: OpsMaxx closes and reopens on the new version.
settings.updatePanel.restartModal.body: Every open SSH session, tunnel and file transfer ends when the app closes. Anything running on a server keeps running there, but OpsMaxx will not be watching it.
settings.updatePanel.downgradeModal.subt: You are running v{{version}}, a beta build.
settings.updatePanel.downgradeModal.body: The newest stable release is probably older than the beta you are on. OpsMaxx will offer it as an update and installing it moves this app down a version, taking the beta-only features with it.
settings.updatePanel.downgradeModal.note: Nothing changes until you install that update, and you can switch back to beta first.

ui.reportBug.cancelled: Report not saved — you cancelled the dialog.
ui.reportBug.recordingToast: Recording. Reproduce the problem, then press the bug button again.
ui.reportBug.title: Report a bug
ui.reportBug.subtitle: Nothing leaves this computer until you save the file and attach it yourself.
ui.reportBug.notCollectedNote: The report could not be collected. Settings → Advanced has the version block to paste by hand.
ui.reportBug.attachNote: Attach the saved file to the issue — do not paste it.
ui.reportBug.recordBodyRecording: The recording was running, and opening this dialog stopped it. Everything the app did between starting it and now is in the report below.
ui.reportBug.recordBody: A report without a recording says what this install is — versions, counts, which features are on — but nothing about what it did. For anything that fails, misbehaves or hangs, press Start recording, make the bug happen again, then press the bug button again. Or send what is below as it stands.
ui.reportBug.readBody: The trace names the internal operations that ran and the errors they raised. Errors routinely carry hostnames, usernames, file paths and command text from your machine and your servers. Passwords, keys and tokens are filtered out before anything is written; a hostname cannot be, because no rule tells one from an ordinary word. Read it, and delete any line you would rather not publish once you have attached it.
ui.reportBug.notCollected: The report could not be collected.
ui.reportBug.attachBody: Save report… writes one text file and opens the issue form with your version and operating system already filled in. Drag the file into the issue — an attachment stays inert, while pasted text is rendered as Markdown and read by automation.
ui.reportBug.savedBody: Saved to {{path}}. The issue form is open in your browser — drag that file into it.
ui.errorBoundary.title: Something broke in the interface
ui.errorBoundary.body: Your servers, credentials and vault are stored on disk and are unaffected. Reloading rebuilds the window — any open SSH sessions will be reconnected.
ui.errorBoundary.footnote: Copy details copies this error exactly as it was thrown, full paths and all — redact hostnames and usernames yourself before posting it. Copy diagnostics is the one to send: it adds your versions and settings, trims paths and strips secrets, and only becomes available once that text is on screen above. It copies that text and nothing else, so glance over it for hostnames first.

settingsPage.knownHosts.title: Trusted SSH host keys
settingsPage.knownHosts.descSome: Connections are refused if a server presents a different key than the one saved here.
settingsPage.knownHosts.descNone: No servers trusted yet — the first connection to a server will ask.
settingsPage.knownHosts.stale.title_one: {{count}} entry is saved against a loopback address
settingsPage.knownHosts.stale.title_othe: {{count}} entries are saved against loopback addresses
settingsPage.knownHosts.stale.desc:
Before 0.36.2, a server reached through a VPN or tunnel had its host key saved under the temporary local address the connection borrowed — a different one every time. That is why those servers kept asking to be trusted again. The entries name no particular machine, so an unrelated local service on the same port would inherit the trust.
If you deliberately trust an SSH server running on this machine, its entry looks the same — remove that one individually instead.
settingsPage.knownHosts.forgotToast: Forgot the saved key for {{host}}. The next connection to it will ask again.
settingsPage.vault.none: No vault on this computer yet
settingsPage.vault.checkingDesc: Reading this machine’s keychain. Nothing is decided until it answers.
settingsPage.vault.noneDesc: A vault holds one copy of each credential and travels inside an encrypted backup. Without one, every server keeps its own.
settingsPage.vault.unlockedDesc: Anything that needs a saved credential can use it until the timer below runs out.
settingsPage.vault.lockedDesc: Anything that needs a saved credential will ask you to unlock first.
settingsPage.vault.unlockReason: Unlocking makes your saved credentials usable again.
settingsPage.vault.heading: Vault
settingsPage.vault.sub: The encrypted store for passwords, SSH keys and API keys.
settingsPage.vault.autoLock.title: Secure after inactivity
settingsPage.vault.autoLock.desc: Clears the vault from this screen and asks for your master password before showing it again. Nothing else stops — connections, background checks, pipeline polling and scheduled backups keep using the credentials in it. The vault locks completely when you quit or your machine sleeps. The timer counts vault inactivity, not time since you started the app, and background work does not postpone it.
settingsPage.vault.touchId.title: Ask for Touch ID when the vault is locked
settingsPage.vault.touchId.desc: Whenever the vault has to be unlocked — opening the Vault, or anything that needs a stored credential — raise the fingerprint prompt without waiting for a click. Cancel it and the master password field is right there. Does nothing unless you have already set up biometric unlock.
settingsPage.debug.title: Debug mode
settingsPage.debug.desc: Record which internal operations run and which fail, so a bug report can say what the app did and not only what it is. You do not need this page to start one — the bug icon in the left rail offers it, which is where a report begins. Those messages come from this machine and your servers, and they routinely name hostnames, usernames, file paths and commands; passwords, keys and tokens are filtered out before anything is written, a hostname cannot be. Nothing is sent anywhere: the trace stays on this computer, you read the whole report before it is written, and starting a new recording clears the old one.
settingsPage.debug.traceSize: {{kb}} KB on disk. Yours to delete whenever you like — reporting a bug does not remove it.
settingsPage.debug.traceSizeCapped: {{kb}} KB on disk, cut at the 8 MB cap. Yours to delete whenever you like — reporting a bug does not remove it.
settingsPage.debug.traceEventsSize: {{events}} events, {{kb}} KB on disk. Yours to delete whenever you like — reporting a bug does not remove it.
settingsPage.debug.traceEventsSizeCapped: {{events}} events, {{kb}} KB on disk, cut at the 8 MB cap. Yours to delete whenever you like — reporting a bug does not remove it.
settingsPage.diagnostics.title: Copy diagnostics
settingsPage.diagnostics.desc: Your app version and update channel, this platform and its Electron, Chrome and Node versions, how many servers, workspaces, databases, tunnels and VPN profiles exist, which optional modules are on, and whether each configurable feature is switched on and actually set up. Counts and on/off states only — no names, hostnames, addresses, usernames, paths or credentials, and nothing read from any server. The crash screen copies this same report with the error text added, which is worth a glance before posting. Nothing is saved to disk.

settingsPage.search.noMatch: No setting matches that. Try a word from what it does — “webhook”, “vault”, “background”.

settingsPage.terminal.heading: Terminal
settingsPage.terminal.closeOnExit.title: Close the pane when the shell exits
settingsPage.terminal.closeOnExit.desc: Typing exit ends the session, so the pane goes with it — the same as every other terminal. A shell that stopped for a reason keeps its pane and says why, whatever this is set to.
settingsPage.terminal.fontFamily.title: Font family
settingsPage.terminal.fontFamily.desc: Monospace font used in the terminal.
settingsPage.terminal.fontSize.title: Font size
settingsPage.terminal.fontSize.desc: Applies to open terminals immediately. Also Ctrl + / Ctrl - / Ctrl 0, or Ctrl+scroll inside a terminal.
settingsPage.terminal.scheme.title: Colour scheme
settingsPage.terminal.scheme.desc: Applies to open terminals immediately. A scheme without its own background keeps the app's, so it follows light and dark.
settingsPage.terminal.cursorBlink.title: Cursor blink
settingsPage.terminal.osc52.title: Let remote programs copy to the clipboard
settingsPage.terminal.osc52.desc: Programs running in a terminal — Claude Code, tmux, Neovim on a server — can put text on this computer's clipboard when you copy inside them. They can only write to it: a request to read your clipboard is never answered. Turn this off to stop any program in a terminal from changing your clipboard.
settingsPage.terminal.shellIntegration.d: Start local shells so they report where each prompt begins and what each command exited with. Uses the shell's own startup options for the session OpsMaxx starts — your shell config files are never modified, and turning this off restores the previous behaviour exactly. zsh and bash get prompt and command marks; fish gets command marks only; a login bash and PowerShell are not supported.
settingsPage.terminal.clickToMove.title: Click to move the cursor
settingsPage.terminal.clickToMove.desc: Click inside the line you are typing to put the shell cursor there. Needs shell integration, so it does nothing in a session without it, and stays out of the way while a command is running or a full-screen program is open.
settingsPage.terminal.localTarget.title: Allow this machine as a target
settingsPage.terminal.localTarget.desc: Open a shell on this computer, and offer it alongside your servers in the Docker, Kubernetes, cron, Files and monitoring panels. When off, every one of those refuses locally and open local file sessions are closed. Never available to the AI bridge either way.
settingsPage.shortcuts.heading: Keyboard Shortcuts
settingsPage.shortcuts.sub: Record a combination by clicking a shortcut. Conflicts are highlighted.
When on, hidden workspaces take their place in the numbering and can be switched to by shortcut. When off, they are skipped and the numbers close up around them.
settingsPage.editor.heading: Editor
settingsPage.editor.sub: How remote files open from the Files view.
settingsPage.editor.external.title: External editor command
settingsPage.editor.external.desc: Run to open a remote file — code for VS Code, subl, nvim, and so on. Leave empty to use the system default for the file type. Saving in the editor uploads the file back automatically.
settingsPage.editor.openExternally.title: Open files externally by default
settingsPage.editor.openExternally.desc: Double-clicking a file in the Files view uses the external editor instead of the built-in inline editor.
settingsPage.monitoring.heading: Monitoring
settingsPage.monitoring.sub: Alerts, background checking, webhook delivery, and the monitor strip.
settingsPage.monitoring.alerts.title: Alerts
settingsPage.monitoring.alerts.desc: The master switch. Covers CPU and memory at or above the threshold, a root filesystem more than 85% full by blocks OR by inodes, a load average at or above 2 per core, and systemd units that have failed — and, since every webhook is sent from an alert, webhook delivery too. CPU, memory and load repeat once a minute while the condition lasts; a full disk or inode table repeats every six hours, or sooner if it gets 5 points worse. They clear themselves on recovery: a filesystem as soon as it is back to 85% or below, CPU and memory once they are 5 points under the threshold, so a server sitting exactly on the line does not flicker on and off. A server that crosses the same line five times in six hours is announced once more and then held quiet until it has gone six hours without crossing again. Anything the server could not measure — no inode accounting, no /proc/loadavg, no df — raises nothing and clears nothing, because a reading nobody could take is not a reading of zero. Switching this off also takes down any alerts already showing.
settingsPage.monitoring.threshold.title: Alert threshold
settingsPage.monitoring.threshold.desc: The same figure applies to CPU and to memory. Disk has its own, fixed at 85%: a root filesystem past that alerts, which is the same 85% at which the Fleet Monitor lists the server as needing attention and turns its disk bar red. Inodes use the same 85% and load its own fixed 2 per core. Only the root filesystem is measured, for blocks and for inodes alike — a server that has filled /var and has room on / raises nothing here.
settingsPage.monitoring.background.title: Check servers in the background
settingsPage.monitoring.background.desc: Sample every server in this workspace on a schedule, even when the monitor is not open, so failures and resource alerts are noticed while you are elsewhere. Opens one SSH exec channel per server per pass, separately from the monitor, so it is real load on the estate rather than a reuse of what is already sampled. Needs the vault unlocked; while it is locked, checking pauses rather than failing.
settingsPage.monitoring.background.keepA: While this is on, each checked server’s connection is held open and never goes idle, so Keep authenticated connection under SSH sessions stops applying to them at any setting. On a server with two-factor authentication that means no new code is requested until you turn this off or quit.
settingsPage.monitoring.howOften.title: How often
settingsPage.monitoring.howOften.desc: Measured from the end of one pass to the start of the next, so a slow estate slows the cadence instead of overlapping checks.
settingsPage.monitoring.dbSize.title: Record how large each database is
settingsPage.monitoring.dbSize.desc: Once an hour, ask each stored database connection for its size and keep the number, so growth can be charted and a disk filling up has a cause beside it. Off by default: unlike a server check, this opens a CONNECTION on the database itself.
settingsPage.monitoring.strip.title: Show monitor under the terminal
settingsPage.monitoring.strip.desc: Live CPU, memory, disk and network docked below the session. Sampling only runs for the visible tab.
settingsPage.ssh.heading: SSH
settingsPage.ssh.jobsDetached.title: Let jobs keep running when the connection drops
settingsPage.ssh.agent.heading: SSH agent
settingsPage.ssh.agent.sub: Other tools on this machine can use the SSH keys in your vault, without a second copy of them sitting in ~/.ssh.
settingsPage.backup.heading: Backup & Restore
settingsPage.backup.sub: Export an encrypted copy of everything, or restore from one.
settingsPage.machineGrants.heading: Works without your master password
settingsPage.machineGrants.sub: Standing permissions that let this machine keep working while nobody is here — and the only place to take one back.
settingsPage.security.heading: Security
settingsPage.security.accessWrite.title: Allow adding and revoking keys on servers
Passwords and key passphrases go to the vault, or to this platform's secure store when no vault is set up. Neither path writes plaintext to disk, and there is no setting that changes it.

settingsPage.credProxy.sub: Let a script or an agent call a third-party API without ever holding the key.

settingsPage.index.compact.desc: Tighter rows and padding across trees, lists and the docked monitor.

settingsPage.index.hiddenWorkspaces.desc: Whether hidden workspaces take their place in the switching numbers.
settingsPage.index.externalEditor.desc: Run to open a remote file — code, subl, nvim, and so on.
settingsPage.index.openExternally.desc: Double-clicking a file uses the external editor instead of the inline one.
settingsPage.index.alerts.desc: The master switch for CPU, memory, disk, inode, load and failed-unit alerts, and for webhook delivery.
settingsPage.index.threshold.desc: The percentage at which CPU and memory alert. Disk and inodes are fixed at 85%, load at 2 per core.
settingsPage.index.background.desc: Sample every server in this workspace on a schedule, even when the monitor is not open, so failures and resource alerts are noticed while you are elsewhere.

settingsPage.index.keychain.desc: Use the platform secure store — never plaintext.
settingsPage.index.confirmDestructive.de: Require confirmation for rm, systemctl stop, etc.
settingsPage.index.credProxy.desc: A local proxy that injects vault credentials into outbound API calls.

modules.fleetSearch.label: Fleet-wide search
modules.fleetSearch.detail: Search systemd units, listening ports and servers across the workspace, from data the monitor already collects.
modules.inventory.label: Inventory
modules.inventory.detail: What every server is — distribution, architecture, CPU, virtualisation — and what it needs: pending updates, security updates where the distribution publishes them, and whether a reboot is owed. Read-only, and nothing is refreshed: package caches are read, never updated, and their age is reported alongside the counts.
modules.patch.label: Patch and update management
modules.patch.detail: What every server needs — pending updates, security updates where the distribution publishes them, and whether a reboot is owed — and applying them in waves, with a health check between waves and a hard refusal to restart a server other servers connect through. It never patches on a schedule and never decides for you.
modules.access.label: Fleet keys and access
modules.access.detail: Which key opens which server and whose it is: every authorized_keys file across the estate, fingerprinted, with locked and expired accounts and administrative group membership alongside. A server whose files could not be read is shown as unreadable and excluded from every count — never as a server with no keys. Reading is the whole of it: nothing on this tab writes to a server, and removing a key is a separate module on the Operations side.
modules.keyRevoke.label: Revoke a key
modules.keyRevoke.detail: Remove one SSH key from every account across the estate that trusts it. Each server takes a timestamped backup, arms its own rollback before OpsMaxx lets go, and keeps the change only once a second, independent session has authenticated against the changed file. Accounts it may not touch are listed by name with the reason, and a key is never reported as gone from an estate that could not be fully read.
modules.capacity.label: Capacity trends
modules.capacity.detail: How full a server is getting and when it runs out — "this disk fills in eleven days" — drawn from the samples the monitor already writes. It stores nothing of its own, schedules nothing and evaluates nothing in the background: every line is derived on demand from history that exists whether or not this is on. A forecast is never stated without the window it was drawn from and how much of that window was sampled. A gap where nothing was measured is left as a hole in the line rather than drawn across; disk and memory are still forecast ACROSS such gaps, because a disk keeps filling while nobody is watching, while CPU is not.
modules.changeLog.label: Change log
modules.changeLog.detail: "What did I change on Tuesday" — one timeline over four records that already exist: shells run on this machine, what you confirmed before a job or a broadcast ran, what an agent did through the MCP bridge, and the alerts, jobs and store events the durable history keeps. Metadata only: commands and targets, never output. It reads; it stores nothing of its own and writes nothing.
modules.rules.label: Rules
modules.rules.detail: When an alert fires, run a job or post to the webhook — with a ceiling on how often it may act. A rule runs the job it was confirmed with, on the servers it was confirmed for, and refuses if either has changed. It is not a workflow language: one trigger, one filter, one action, one rate limit.
modules.drift.label: Configuration drift
modules.drift.detail: Compare a watched configuration file across the estate and say where it diverges — "all twelve web servers have this nginx.conf, three do not". Every file is compared under normalisation rules that are named on screen, so two files that differ and are called the same say which rule ate the difference. A server that could not be read is never reported as a server that matches. Read-only: it never writes a file back to bring a server into line.
modules.posture.label: Security posture
modules.posture.detail: What every server already knows about its own exposure: which firewall is active and the shape of its rules, whether SELinux or AppArmor is enforcing, how sshd compares with a hardening baseline, and how many logins have failed. Read-only, and emphatically not a vulnerability scanner — the pending security update count comes from the Inventory probe, which asks the server's own package manager, rather than from a CVE feed. A check that could not run is shown as unread, never as passed.
modules.broadcast.label: Run a command on many servers
modules.broadcast.detail: Run one command across selected servers, with confirmation that scales to how many servers and how dangerous the command is.
modules.httpChecks.label: Service checks
modules.httpChecks.detail: Watch any URL from the outside and see whether it answers, how fast, and how often it has been up. External on purpose: a server can be perfectly healthy while the service in front of it returns 502.
modules.netTools.label: Network tools
modules.netTools.detail: Run ping and traceroute from this machine or from any server. "Can this server reach that service" is a different question from "can my laptop reach it", and it is usually the one that matters.
modules.logTail.label: Live log tailing
modules.logTail.detail: Follow a systemd unit or a log file on several servers at once, interleaved by server.
modules.cron.label: Scheduled jobs
modules.cron.detail: Read crontabs, /etc/cron.d and systemd timers across the estate, and say which of those sources this account was actually allowed to read. Read-only: changing a schedule is a write, and it lives on the Operations side under Jobs.
modules.jobs.label: Jobs
modules.jobs.detail: Compose a multi-step job, pick the servers, run it in waves and watch it. Every job asks for the confirmation its own risk demands, and the answer is recorded before anything runs.
modules.services.label: Server services
modules.services.detail: Read what each server supervises for your account with `systemd --user` — what is running, what has failed, and whether it survives you logging out. Read-only: nothing is started, stopped or written, and installing a new unit is a write that lives on the Operations side under Jobs.
modules.processes.label: Local processes
modules.processes.detail: Run, watch, restart and read the logs of a long-lived process on THIS machine — a dev server, a worker, a script that should outlive its terminal. Restart policies, exponential backoff, crash-loop detection and a bounded log ring, from the supervisor that already keeps VPN engines alive. Nothing runs on a remote server, nothing starts by itself, and a value that looks like a secret has to come from the vault rather than the process list.
modules.docker.label: Docker
modules.docker.detail: List containers on a server, read their logs, and open a shell inside a running one. Uses the docker binary already on the server — a container shell is arbitrary code execution there.
modules.cicd.label: CI/CD
modules.cicd.detail: Connect a Jenkins, GitLab or GitHub Actions account and read what it did: pipelines, run history, and the log of the step that failed, beside the server the run changed. This module reads only. Starting a build, cancelling one, and enabling or disabling a job are the separate "Start a build" module, and its controls appear on this tab only while that one is switched on.
modules.cicdTrigger.label: Start a build
modules.cicdTrigger.detail: Start, re-run and cancel builds on a CI server OpsMaxx does not administer, and enable or disable a job. What runs is the pipeline definition already in that repository — not anything composed here — so it can deploy, migrate or restart whatever that file says. Once a run has started OpsMaxx cannot stop it: cancelling is a request to a third party that may already have finished.
modules.kubernetes.label: Kubernetes
modules.kubernetes.detail: List contexts, namespaces and pods and read pod logs, using the kubectl already on the server. Reading only: it never switches your context, never execs into a pod, and never applies or deletes anything.
modules.addy.label: Sync & devices
modules.addy.detail: Your own machines, and what has reached them. OpsMaxx can carry servers, workspaces, tunnels and the vault between your devices through an addy relay you run yourself — every object sealed before it leaves, and the relay holding no key. This panel is the readout and the way in: which relay this device is enrolled on, which devices are on the account, and when anything last synced. It reads only, and it touches no server in the estate.
monitor.access.keyCount.unreadableTitle_: {{count}} line in this file could not be fingerprinted, so it is not in the count beside it and cannot be matched against other servers.
{{count}} lines in this file could not be fingerprinted, so they are not in the count beside it and cannot be matched against other servers.
monitor.access.keyCount.rootTitle: Read as root after the unprivileged attempt was refused.
monitor.access.title: Keys and access
monitor.access.about: Which SSH keys can reach which servers, and which accounts they land on. Files are read, never edited, and no private key is touched.
monitor.access.export.csvTitle: Every account and key across this estate as a CSV, with a coverage section naming every host that could not be read and every sshd that reads keys from somewhere this did not look.
monitor.access.export.jsonTitle: The same review as JSON, coverage first.

monitor.alerts.outstanding.quietSub: Anything that has been raised and cleared is in the history below.
monitor.alerts.how.summary: How alerting works — where each kind comes from, and what a snooze does
monitor.alerts.how.dbVerdicts: Database verdicts are not listed under Outstanding and cannot be snoozed: they are occurrences rather than conditions, so there is no repeat to stop. Every one is in the history below.
monitor.alerts.how.dwell_one: CPU, memory and load have to stay over the line for {{count}} minute — and be read at least {{samples}} times in that period — before anything is said. A compile or a log rotation takes a host to 100% for a few seconds, and that is not an incident. The status-bar chip still follows every reading, so nothing is hidden; the all-clear waits the same {{count}} minute, so one quiet sample on a host that is still busy does not close an alert that is still true. Disk, inodes and certificates have no wait: they do not move between two samples, and delaying them would buy nothing.
monitor.alerts.how.dwell_other: CPU, memory and load have to stay over the line for {{count}} minutes — and be read at least {{samples}} times in that period — before anything is said. A compile or a log rotation takes a host to 100% for a few seconds, and that is not an incident. The status-bar chip still follows every reading, so nothing is hidden; the all-clear waits the same {{count}} minutes, so one quiet sample on a host that is still busy does not close an alert that is still true. Disk, inodes and certificates have no wait: they do not move between two samples, and delaying them would buy nothing.
monitor.alerts.how.snoozing: Snoozing stops this app talking about one host-and-kind for a while and leaves the status-bar chip up, because the condition has not changed. Acknowledging takes it out of Outstanding entirely and says nothing more until the condition itself clears, however long that takes.
monitor.alerts.thresholds.summary: Per-server thresholds — CPU and memory, where the estate is not uniform
monitor.alerts.thresholds.desc: The CPU and memory line for one server, where the estate is not uniform — a build box at 95% is working and a database at 95% is in trouble. Blank uses the workspace default of {{threshold}}%. Disk, inodes and load are deliberately not settable per server: they are the numbers the Fleet Monitor colours a bar at and lists a server under, and an alert firing at a different number from the screen it sends you to is worse than no alert.

addy.panel.about: Your own machines, and what has reached them. OpsMaxx carries servers, workspaces, tunnels and the vault between your devices through an addy relay you run yourself — every object is sealed before it leaves and the relay holds no key. Nothing here reads or changes a server.

addy.transfers.title: Files
addy.transfers.desc: Send a file to one of your other machines. It is sealed before it leaves and the relay cannot read it; it waits there if that machine is asleep. Anything sent here lands in a folder OpsMaxx keeps and is deleted after a week.
addy.rekey.title: Change the account key
addy.rekey.desc: Removing a device stops it receiving anything new. It does not take back the key that device already has, so a machine that was stolen rather than retired can still read everything it had. This replaces that key and re-seals every collection under the new one.
addy.rekey.needsPhrase: It needs your recovery phrase. The key being replaced is the one the removed device is holding, so it cannot be the one that signs the replacement.
addy.rekey.waiting_one: {{count}} set-aside copy is still waiting for a decision, and re-keying deletes it. Decide on it first with Review now.
addy.rekey.waiting_other: {{count}} set-aside copies are still waiting for a decision, and re-keying deletes them. Decide on them first with Review now.
addy.rekey.done_one: The account key was changed. {{count}} item was re-sealed under the new one — your other devices pick it up the next time they sync. Then check that Account fingerprint shows the same words on each of them.
addy.rekey.done_other: The account key was changed. {{count}} items were re-sealed under the new one — your other devices pick it up the next time they sync. Then check that Account fingerprint shows the same words on each of them.
addy.pause.paused: Sync paused. It starts again next time OpsMaxx opens.
addy.pause.pauseDesc: Stops carrying data between your devices without leaving the account. Your keys stay, the other devices are not told, and sync starts again the next time OpsMaxx opens.
addy.pause.resumeDesc: Nothing is being carried between your devices right now. Your account and keys are untouched.
addy.leave.notOnAccount: This device was not on an account.
addy.leave.leftAndRemoved: This device has left the account and removed itself from your device list.
addy.leave.leftNotRemoved: This device has left the account, but could not remove itself from your device list — remove it from one of your other devices.
addy.leave.leftNotRemovedBecause: This device has left the account, but could not remove itself from your device list ({{problem}}) — remove it from one of your other devices.
addy.leave.title: Leave this account
addy.leave.desc: Stops sync on this machine and forgets the keys it holds. Your servers, workspaces, tunnels and vault stay exactly as they are here — what goes is this device's ability to read anything further from the relay.
addy.leave.descAt: Stops sync on this machine and forgets the keys it holds. Your servers, workspaces, tunnels and vault stay exactly as they are here — what goes is this device's ability to read anything further from {{relay}}.
addy.leave.roster: It also removes this device from your device list, if it can reach the relay. If it cannot, the other machines keep listing it until somebody there removes it.
addy.leave.alone: This is the only device on the account. After this, the twelve-word recovery phrase is the only way back into it — the relay holds no key and cannot help.
addy.leave.notAlone: Nothing changes for the other devices; they keep syncing with each other.
addy.leave.rejoin: Joining again — this relay or a different one — starts from the setup screen.
addy.clipboard.title: Send and receive the clipboard with a keystroke
addy.clipboard.desc:
Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+C sends what is on this clipboard to your other devices; Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+V puts the newest thing sent to this one onto the clipboard. Nothing is mirrored in the background — a clipboard that copied everything would send the password you just copied to every machine you own.
These are taken from every application while OpsMaxx is running, and Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+C is the developer tools in most browsers.
addy.clipboard.blockedHelp: Close it, or quit whatever has the combination, and switch this off and on again.
addy.clipboard.notAttached: Not active until this device reaches the relay.

addy.fingerprint.desc: A machine recovering this account with the recovery phrase shows five words before it joins. They must be these, in this order. If they differ, tell it to stop.

addy.setup.phrase.desc: These twelve words are the only way back into this account if you lose every device on it. OpsMaxx cannot show them to you again — it keeps no copy. OpsMaxx clears them from the clipboard after a minute if nothing else has been copied since.

ai.overview.intro: Let AI agents like Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and other MCP-compatible clients operate your servers through OpsMaxx — without ever seeing an SSH password, private key or database credential. OpsMaxx resolves the friendly names, enforces access-group policy and asks for your approval on anything sensitive.
ai.overview.step1: Pick a profile — Read only, Ask first, Auto (routine work runs, risky actions ask) or Bypass; or Custom, to use an access group instead.
ai.overview.step2: Create an AI Agent session scoped to one or more workspaces with that profile, and copy its token.
ai.overview.step3: Point Claude Code, Codex or another MCP client at OpsMaxx's local MCP server with that token.
ai.overview.step4: Approve or deny actions as they come up — the AI waits for your answer.
ai.overview.optional: Optional: under Access Groups, hold a workspace or server below every session's group with an assignment, or mark it Protected so agents there are held at Ask first — for production.
ai.overview.connectHint: Connect an agent above does steps 1–4 in one click. Codex and Gemini CLI are still wired up by hand — {{command}}, or the snippet under AI Agents.

ai.audit.outcome.notAskedDetail: OpsMaxx did not ask anyone about this request, and it did not run.
ai.audit.outcome.readOnlyDetail: Refused in Read only mode. Nothing was asked.
ai.audit.outcome.groupRefusedError: The access group refused this: {{error}} Nothing was asked.
ai.audit.outcome.groupRefusedDetail: The access group refused this. Nothing was asked.
ai.audit.outcome.becauseApprovedSession: You approved this request, and allowed the same on this server for the rest of the session.
ai.audit.outcome.becauseApprovedEarlier: Nothing was asked: an approval given earlier in this session covered it.
ai.audit.outcome.becauseBypassed: Ran without asking: session in Bypass mode. The policy would otherwise have asked or refused.
ai.audit.outcome.becauseAllowed: The access group allowed this outright, so nothing was asked.

ai.audit.outcome.thenBlockedDetail: {{because}} It was then refused by a path rule or a capability the group does not grant.

monitor.rules.empty.body: Press New rule to connect an alert to a job or to the webhook. Every rule is confirmed once, against a specific job and specific servers, and refuses to run if either of those changes afterwards.
monitor.patch.error.noKernel: This build cannot read kernels. Restart the app to rebuild it.
monitor.patch.error.noSecurityList: This build cannot list security updates. Restart the app to rebuild it.
monitor.patch.title: Patch and updates
monitor.patch.about: Choose the servers to update, review the plan, then run it in waves. Nothing installs until you confirm, and there is no unattended mode.
monitor.patch.selectNeedyTitle: Selects the servers that report something to install or a reboot they are owed. A server whose counts could not be read is NOT selected here: it is unknown, not known to need something, and picking it would be this screen deciding something for you. The button beside this one offers those servers separately.
monitor.patch.addUnknownTitle: Adds the servers where at least one question had no answer — a count that could not be read, a security channel that does not exist, a reboot flag nothing could check. They are unknown, not known to be clean, and nothing here can tell you which. Adding them to the selection is a decision for you to make deliberately.
monitor.patch.checkNowTitle: Sweeps the estate now and re-reads what has already been collected. Nothing is installed and no package cache is refreshed by this.
monitor.patch.empty.subject: No server facts have been collected yet.
monitor.patch.empty.note: Update counts come from the same hourly sweep the inventory reads. Nothing is installed and no package cache is refreshed.
monitor.patch.unanswerable_one: {{count}} server can never report a security update count, so it is not in the {{total}} above. Treat it as unknown, never as zero.
monitor.patch.unanswerable_other: {{count}} servers can never report a security update count, so they are not in the {{total}} above. Treat them as unknown, never as zero.
monitor.patch.unanswerableWhyBody: Arch and Alpine have no security channel at all, and dnf cannot answer where the repositories publish no updateinfo.
monitor.patch.plan.healthGate: hold between waves until the estate looks healthy
monitor.patch.plan.reboot: restart the servers that say they need it
monitor.patch.plan.gateUnavailable: The wave gate is unavailable. {{note}} Until it is on, the waves below roll on one after another with nothing checking the estate in between — run them in small waves and watch, or turn the sampler on first.
monitor.patch.bar.restarting_one: {{count}} wave, restarting the hosts that say they need it
monitor.patch.bar.restarting_other: {{count}} waves, restarting the hosts that say they need it
monitor.patch.confirm.run_one: This will run on {{hosts}} in {{count}} wave.
monitor.patch.confirm.run_other: This will run on {{hosts}} in {{count}} waves.
monitor.patch.confirm.runRestart_one: This will run on {{hosts}} in {{count}} wave, restarting the servers that say they need it.
monitor.patch.confirm.runRestart_other: This will run on {{hosts}} in {{count}} waves, restarting the servers that say they need it.
