monitor.capacity.fill.inodesWithinDay: Out of inodes within a day
monitor.capacity.headline.noCeiling: No ceiling — a CPU does not fill up
monitor.capacity.headline.overThreshold: At or over its threshold now
monitor.capacity.basis.disk: of the root filesystem, as df reports it
monitor.capacity.card.sparkLabel_one: {{label}}: the last {{count}} reading, without the gaps
monitor.capacity.card.sparkLabel_other: {{label}}: the last {{count}} readings, without the gaps
monitor.capacity.card.bytesBasis: Measured in bytes, not in percent: df reports capacity as a rounded whole number, so a large filesystem sits still for weeks and then moves a whole point at once. As a percentage the same disk reads: {{forecast}}
monitor.capacity.chart.label: {{label}} over the last {{span}}
monitor.capacity.chart.gapNotRunning: OpsMaxx was not running for {{span}} — nothing was measured across it, so the line is broken there rather than joined.
monitor.capacity.chart.gapUnknown: No samples for {{span}}. The line is broken there rather than joined — nothing was measured across it.
monitor.capacity.method.summary: How a date is worked out, and when one is refused
monitor.capacity.method.line: Every projection is a straight line — an ordinary least-squares fit through the samples in the window, extended until it meets the threshold. It assumes the current rate holds, and that assumption is doing most of the work: treat a date as a description of today’s rate, not as a schedule.
monitor.capacity.method.refusals: Nothing is projected from fewer than {{points}} samples, from a run shorter than {{span}}, or from points that sit further from the line than an r² of {{r2}} allows. If one jump accounts for {{share}}% or more of the whole rise, that is something written once and not a trend, and no date is given. Crossings further out than {{days}} days are not stated at all.
monitor.capacity.method.source: Nothing is measured for this screen. Every number is derived on demand from samples the fleet sampler already wrote, which is also why a host that has just been added has no history to draw on.
monitor.capacity.storage.vaultReason: Reading this host’s filesystems needs its stored credential.
monitor.capacity.storage.noBridge: This build cannot read filesystems. Restart the app to rebuild it.
monitor.capacity.about: What is going to run out on this server, and when — projected from samples the fleet sampler already writes. Nothing extra is measured for this panel.
monitor.capacity.refreshTitle: Re-reads the samples already collected for this window. New samples arrive with the hourly sweep.
monitor.capacity.noBridge: This build’s preload does not expose capacity trends yet. Restart the app to rebuild it.
monitor.capacity.noServers.title: No servers to chart.
monitor.capacity.noServers.body: Add a server to this workspace and its samples start accumulating here.
monitor.capacity.storeFailed: Could not read the history store.
monitor.capacity.noHistory.subject: No stored history.
monitor.capacity.noHistory.note: Trends are drawn from the sampler’s own samples. Nothing is measured for this panel, so it fills only while background checking is running.
monitor.capacity.nothingSampled.subject: Nothing has been sampled for {{name}} in this window.
monitor.capacity.nothingSampled.note: A longer window will not help until sampling resumes — the store has no readings for this host at any resolution.
monitor.capacity.noneUrgent: Nothing here is heading for a limit within {{days}} days. None of the {{total}} metrics produced a date — the reason for each is below.
monitor.capacity.quietSummary: No date for {{quiet}} of {{total}} — open for the reason each was refused
monitor.capacity.storeNote: The store keeps {{fullDays}} days of {{full}} and {{retainedDays}} days of {{hourly}}. Older than that is gone, which is why a longer window is not always more line.
monitor.capacity.storage.rootOnly: The disk row above is the root filesystem. This host may have others.
monitor.capacity.storage.failed: The filesystems could not be read: {{error}}
monitor.posture.fw.inactiveHelp: {{tool}} is switched off and the kernel filter tables were read and are empty. Both halves were checked; this server is not filtering.
monitor.posture.fw.noRulesHelp: {{tool}} was read and lists no rules at all. This is a reading, not a gap.
monitor.posture.fw.backendRules_one: The kernel tables underneath ({{backend}}) hold {{count}} rule.
monitor.posture.fw.backendRules_other: The kernel tables underneath ({{backend}}) hold {{count}} rules.
monitor.posture.fw.backendUnread: The kernel tables underneath ({{backend}}) hold an unread number of rules.
monitor.posture.mac.noneHelp: Neither SELinux nor AppArmor is on this server, and that was checked rather than assumed. Plenty of estates run this way deliberately.
monitor.posture.mac.selinuxDriftHelp: SELinux is {{mode}} right now, and /etc/selinux/config says {{bootMode}}. The running mode and the boot-time setting disagree, so this server changes behaviour at its next reboot.
monitor.posture.mac.apparmorDisabledHelp: The AppArmor module is present and switched off.
monitor.posture.mac.apparmorNotReadHelp: {{help}} AppArmor is enabled and its profile list needs root here, so how many profiles merely complain is unknown — and a complaining profile enforces nothing.
monitor.posture.mac.profilesHelp: {{profiles}} profiles are loaded and {{complain}} of them are in complain mode, which logs rather than blocks.
monitor.posture.sshd.partialHelp: {{read}} of {{total}} directives were read and none of them is weak. The other {{unread}} were not read at all
monitor.posture.sshd.partialHelpFiles: {{read}} of {{total}} directives were read and none of them is weak. The other {{unread}} were not read at all — this reading came from configuration files rather than from sshd itself, so a directive nobody wrote down is decided by a compiled-in default this probe cannot see. Passwordless sudo lets `sshd -T` answer exactly.
monitor.posture.sshd.cleanHelp: Every directive in the baseline was read from sshd’s effective configuration and none of them is weak.
monitor.posture.failed.helpNamed: {{count}} failed attempts naming {{users}} distinct accounts, from {{source}}{{window}}.
monitor.posture.oom.help_one: The kernel reaped {{count}} process for memory, read from {{source}}. Counts only: a process name is a string the process chose for itself.
monitor.posture.oom.help_other: The kernel reaped {{count}} processes for memory, read from {{source}}. Counts only: a process name is a string the process chose for itself.
monitor.posture.oom.helpNamed_one: The kernel reaped {{count}} process for memory, under {{names}}, read from {{source}}. Counts only: a process name is a string the process chose for itself.
monitor.posture.oom.helpNamed_other: The kernel reaped {{count}} processes for memory, under {{names}}, read from {{source}}. Counts only: a process name is a string the process chose for itself.
monitor.posture.oom.noneInHelp: The kernel journal was asked for the last {{hours}} hours and holds no OOM kill. This is a reading over a stated window, not a gap.
monitor.posture.oom.noWindowSource: a source with no stated window
monitor.posture.oom.unboundedHelp: {{help}} This was read from {{source}}, which is not a period of time — it holds as much as it holds. Nothing was found in it, and that is NOT a report of no OOM kills in the last day. Passwordless sudo lets journalctl -k answer over a real window.
monitor.posture.cert.bound: Searched {{roots}} to {{depth}} levels, at most {{files}} files, without crossing filesystems.
monitor.posture.cert.dirsRefusedHelp: A certificate directory that could not be entered is NOT a directory with no certificates. /etc/letsencrypt is 0700 root on most servers, so this usually closes with passwordless sudo. {{bound}}
monitor.posture.cert.unreadHelp_one: {{count}} file was found and could not be dated — unreadable, not a certificate, or DER this build will not parse. A certificate that could not be parsed is not a certificate that is valid. {{bound}}
monitor.posture.cert.unreadHelp_other: {{count}} files were found and could not be dated — unreadable, not a certificate, or DER this build will not parse. A certificate that could not be parsed is not a certificate that is valid. {{bound}}
monitor.posture.cert.noDirsHelp: None of the directories OpsMaxx looks in exists on this server, and that was checked rather than assumed. {{bound}}
monitor.posture.cert.noneFoundHelp: Every directory was read and holds no certificate. This is a reading, not a gap — and it is not the same as "this server is fine", because nothing here has an expiry to be near. {{bound}}
monitor.posture.cert.expiredHelp: The soonest certificate on this server expired {{days}} days ago. This is an outage in progress, not a warning.
monitor.posture.cert.leftHelp: The soonest certificate on this server has {{days}} days left.
monitor.posture.cert.leftSoonHelp: The soonest certificate on this server has {{days}} days left, which is inside the {{line}}-day line certbot itself renews at — the renewal that should have run has not.
monitor.posture.cert.missingHelp_one: {{count}} other thing could not be read, so this number may not be the worst one on the server.
monitor.posture.cert.missingHelp_other: {{count}} other things could not be read, so this number may not be the worst one on the server.
monitor.posture.updates.noneHelp: The package manager was asked and reports no pending security updates. Collected by the Inventory probe, not recomputed here.
monitor.posture.updates.countHelp_one: {{count}} pending security update, as this server's own package manager counts them. Collected by the Inventory probe.
monitor.posture.updates.countHelp_other: {{count}} pending security updates, as this server's own package manager counts them. Collected by the Inventory probe.
monitor.posture.rules.nothingRead: Nothing was read about this server’s firewall at all.
monitor.posture.rules.nothingReadDetail: Nothing was read about this server’s firewall at all — {{detail}}.
monitor.posture.rules.notRequested: The rule lines were not collected for this server, and this space is therefore not a statement about what it lets in. The capability Firewall rules: the addresses and ports this server accepts is not granted to the access group that governs this server, so OpsMaxx never asked for them. Grant it in AI access if you want them; the counts above are unaffected either way.
monitor.posture.rules.refused: The rule lines could not be read on this server, which is not a report of an empty ruleset. Most of these close with passwordless sudo for the account OpsMaxx connects as.
monitor.posture.rules.refusedDetail: The rule lines could not be read on this server, which is not a report of an empty ruleset. Collector said: {{detail}}. Most of these close with passwordless sudo for the account OpsMaxx connects as.
monitor.posture.rules.front: What the firewall front end lists
monitor.posture.rules.kernel: What the kernel tables underneath hold
monitor.posture.rules.truncated: · showing {{shown}} of {{matched}}, cut at {{max}} lines on the server
monitor.posture.rules.empty: This was read and lists nothing. That is a reading, not a gap — and on its own it is not “this server is closed”: the other reading, and anything in front of the NIC, are separate questions.
monitor.posture.col.firewallHelp: Which firewall is active and how many rules it lists. Both the front end and the kernel tables underneath are read, because "ufw is inactive" is not "nothing is filtering".
monitor.posture.col.macHelp: Whether mandatory access control is enforcing. A server with neither is a finding, not a gap — and it is shown differently from a server that could not be asked.
monitor.posture.col.sshdHelp: Seven directives against a hardening baseline. A directive that could not be read is never counted as passing.
monitor.posture.col.failedHelp: How many failed attempts the server recorded and how many distinct account names they tried. Counts only: every field on a failed-login record is text an attacker chose.
monitor.posture.col.updatesHelp: Pending security updates as the server’s own package manager counts them. Collected by the Inventory probe and shown here unchanged — OpsMaxx computes nothing from a CVE feed.
monitor.posture.col.oomHelp: Processes the kernel reaped for memory in the last 24 hours. Only the journal can be asked for a window — a count read from dmesg or kern.log is real, and a ZERO read from either is not a statement about a day and is not drawn as one.
monitor.posture.col.certsHelp: Days left on the soonest certificate in a bounded set of named directories on this server. Not a TLS scanner: nothing is fetched over the network, the distribution trust store is deliberately not searched, and a directory that could not be entered is never rendered as a server with no certificates.
monitor.posture.notRead.offlineLead: Offline — nothing was read from this server.
monitor.posture.notRead.offlineWords: That is one server nobody could reach, not a row of checks that failed on it. None of them passed either: this row is empty because the server did not answer, and it says nothing about how the server is configured. It will be read on the first sweep after it comes back.
monitor.posture.notRead.failedLead: The posture probe failed here, so nothing was read.
monitor.posture.notRead.failedWords: One probe failed; the checks in this row never ran, and none of them is clear. The reason the probe gave is above this table.
monitor.posture.notRead.pendingWords: This server is reachable and the background sweep has not got to it. There is nothing here yet — that is the absence of a finding rather than a finding, and nothing on this server is waiting to be configured. Press Check now to read it straight away; if it stays empty, background checking may be switched off in Settings.
monitor.posture.notRead.inventory_one: Its last inventory counted {{count}} pending security update — that one number is the Inventory probe’s, read at some earlier point, and it is not a posture reading.
monitor.posture.notRead.inventory_other: Its last inventory counted {{count}} pending security updates — that one number is the Inventory probe’s, read at some earlier point, and it is not a posture reading.
monitor.posture.checkNowTitle: Collects posture from every server now, ignoring the hourly clock. Nothing is changed by this: no firewall is enabled, no SELinux mode is set and no configuration is written.
monitor.posture.about: Firewalls, SELinux and AppArmor, sshd settings, OOM kills and certificate expiry, per server. Everything is read; no firewall is enabled and no configuration is written.
monitor.posture.empty.subject: No security posture has been collected yet.
monitor.posture.empty.note: Firewalls are read, never enabled; SELinux modes are read, never set; no configuration file is written.
monitor.posture.stats.sshdUnknown: · {{count}} sshd config could not be read
monitor.posture.stats.oomUnknown: · {{count}} kernel log could not be read over a stated window
monitor.posture.unknownNote_one: {{count}} check across this estate could not run, and a check that could not run is not a check that passed. Those servers are not in the counts above and they are not clear.
monitor.posture.unknownNote_other: {{count}} checks across this estate could not run, and a check that could not run is not a check that passed. Those servers are not in the counts above and they are not clear.
monitor.posture.notReadHosts_one: {{count}} host here was not read at all — every check on it is in that number, and its row says why.
monitor.posture.notReadHosts_other: {{count}} hosts here were not read at all — every check on them is in that number, and their rows say why.
monitor.posture.howToCloseBody: Most of these close with passwordless sudo for the account OpsMaxx connects as, which lets the probe read a ruleset and ask sshd for its effective configuration. Nothing about that grants any write.
monitor.posture.row.offlineTitle: This server is offline now. Everything in this row was read before it stopped answering.
monitor.posture.row.sshdTitle: Show every directive in the hardening baseline, including the ones that could not be read.
monitor.posture.row.rulesTitle: The rule lines this server’s firewall lists, as it printed them — or the reason there are none to show. Collected only where the Firewall rules capability is granted.
monitor.posture.sshdDetail.effective: Read from sshd’s own effective configuration.
monitor.posture.sshdDetail.files: Read from configuration files, not from sshd. A directive nobody wrote down is decided by a compiled-in default this probe cannot see, so it is shown as unread rather than guessed.
monitor.posture.sshdDetail.matchBlocks_o: This configuration has {{count}} conditional <mono>Match</mono> block. The values below are the global ones; a connection matching one of those blocks gets different answers.
This configuration has {{count}} conditional <mono>Match</mono> blocks. The values below are the global ones; a connection matching one of those blocks gets different answers.
monitor.logTail.unlockReason: Tailing logs needs each server’s stored credential.
monitor.logTail.noPauseBridge: This build cannot pause a tail — the pause bridge is not wired.
monitor.logTail.title: Log tail
monitor.logTail.about: Follows a systemd unit, a file or a container’s output across the servers you pick, interleaved into one stream. A server that refuses is named rather than left out.
monitor.logTail.selectServer: Select a server to load the list
monitor.logTail.pauseTitle: Hold the stream without closing the connection
monitor.logTail.nothingMatches: Nothing matches what you have typed.
monitor.logTail.sudoTitle: This server refused the unprivileged read, so it was retried with sudo -n
monitor.logTail.paused: paused, the server is still being followed
monitor.logTail.emptyPick: Pick one or more servers above, name a unit, file or container, then press Tail.
monitor.logTail.emptyNameUnit: Name a unit above, then press Tail.
monitor.logTail.emptyNameFile: Name a file path above, then press Tail.
monitor.logTail.emptyNameContainer: Name a container above, then press Tail.
monitor.logTail.emptyStream: Lines from every selected server arrive in one stream, colour-coded by server, and the filter accepts text, <mono>/regex/</mono> or <mono>!exclude</mono>.
monitor.broadcast.title: Run a command
monitor.broadcast.about: Runs one command on every server you pick, one connection each. Nothing runs until you confirm, and a command that changes or destroys state says so before the dialog opens.
monitor.broadcast.placeholder: Command to run on the selected servers…
monitor.broadcast.noneOnline: No server in this workspace is online.
monitor.broadcast.unlockReason: Running a command on these servers needs their stored credentials.
monitor.broadcast.stopTitle: Hosts that have not started will not start. A host already running is left to finish — killing it mid-write is how a change ends up half applied.
monitor.broadcast.refusedOne: {{name}} refused this command for this account.
monitor.broadcast.refusedMany: {{count}} servers refused this command for this account.
monitor.broadcast.refusedSudo: Nothing was retried as root. Prefixing the command with <mono>sudo</mono> will re-run it here — and will ask you to confirm again, because running as root across several servers is a bigger thing than running it as yourself.
monitor.broadcast.emptyPick: Pick the servers to run on from the row above, type a command, then press Run.
monitor.broadcast.emptySelected_one: {{count}} server selected. Type a command above, then press Run.
monitor.broadcast.emptySelected_other: {{count}} servers selected. Type a command above, then press Run.
monitor.broadcast.emptyResults: Results appear here, one block per server, and a server that refuses is reported rather than retried as root.
monitor.changeLog.tile.humanSub: done by a person at this app
monitor.changeLog.coverageFull: All four records were read in full for this window.
monitor.changeLog.coverage.truncated: one was read only back to a point
monitor.changeLog.coverage.unparsed: one had lines that would not parse
monitor.changeLog.coverageIncomplete: This timeline is NOT complete: of four records, {{missing}}. What is missing is listed here.
monitor.changeLog.about: What OpsMaxx itself changed on the estate, and when — with the coverage of each source stated, so a quiet window is not read as a quiet week.
monitor.changeLog.unavailable: The change log could not be read: this window is newer than the preload script it booted with. Restart the app to rebuild it. Nothing below is a statement about what happened.
monitor.changeLog.pageCut: at least — the page was cut
monitor.changeLog.noServerNamed: none of this names a server
monitor.changeLog.unattributed: {{count}} entries in this window name no server at all — a local shell, or a job that had not reached one — so filtering by server hides them. They are not absent; they are unattributed.
monitor.changeLog.more: More entries matched than fit on one page. The oldest shown is {{oldest}}; narrow the window to see further back.
monitor.changeLog.emptyTitle: Nothing matched this window — read the coverage above before reading that as a quiet period.
monitor.changeLog.emptyBody: Widening the time range, or clearing the server filter, is the next thing to try.
monitor.netTools.notProbeable: That is not a host this can probe.
monitor.netTools.chooseSource: Choose where to run this from.
monitor.netTools.noBridge: This build of the bridge cannot run network tools.
monitor.netTools.couldNotRun: The command could not be run.
monitor.netTools.sub: Run ping and traceroute from this machine or from a server
monitor.netTools.hostHint: Enter a hostname or an IP address. Anything else is refused before a command is built.
monitor.httpMonitor.sub: Watch any URL from the outside
monitor.httpMonitor.urlHint: Enter a full http:// or https:// URL.
monitor.httpMonitor.emptyMessage: Watch a URL to see whether it answers, how fast, and how often it has been up while this view is open.
monitor.httpMonitor.sessionNote: Checks run while this view is open and their history is kept for this session. They do not run in the background and do not raise alerts yet.

monitor.services.unlockReason: Reading what each server supervises needs its stored credential.
monitor.services.noServersTitle: This workspace has no servers to ask.
monitor.services.readingTitle_one: Reading {{count}} server. Each is asked over its own connection, so this takes longer on a large estate.
monitor.services.readingTitle_other: Reading {{count}} servers. Each is asked over its own connection, so this takes longer on a large estate.
monitor.services.readTitle: Asks each server in this workspace what its own systemd is supervising for your account. Read-only.
monitor.services.about: What each server’s own systemd supervises for your account. Read-only — nothing is started, stopped or written here, because the server’s supervisor is the one that is still there when OpsMaxx is not. Installing a unit writes a file onto a host, so it lives on the Operations rail.
monitor.services.noServersBody: A server belongs to one workspace, and this panel only asks the active one’s. Add a server to this workspace, or switch to the workspace yours are in from the picker beside the app name in the title bar.
monitor.services.readingBody: Each is asked over its own connection, so a large estate takes a moment. Servers that are unreachable or have no systemd are reported rather than skipped.
monitor.services.pressRead: Press Read services to ask each server what it is supervising for you.
monitor.services.locked: Not read — this server’s credential is in the locked vault.
monitor.services.installTitle: Opens Operations › Jobs › Install a service, with this server chosen. Writing a unit file changes a server, so it lives on the rail where everything does.

ai.security.cliTitle: Or skip typing tokens: the OpsMaxx CLI launcher
ai.security.cliDesc: Install the CLI once (<install/>, or <installLocal/> from this repo), then run <claude/> or <codex/>. The first run pops a one-time pairing code right here in OpsMaxx — type it into the terminal and the session, token and MCP config are wired up for you. <run/> works the same way for any other MCP-aware CLI.

ai.connect.intro: Turns on the bridge, creates a session across your workspaces and hands it to the client. The session does not expire — revoke it under Active Sessions.

ai.connect.accessGroupDesc: The Custom profile does exactly what this group says.

ai.sessionAccess.summary.readOnly: Read only: it can look at everything, and every change is refused.
ai.sessionAccess.summary.ask: Ask first: it can look at everything, and every change is asked for before it runs.
ai.sessionAccess.summary.auto: Auto: routine work runs without asking; sudo and risky actions — destructive commands, database writes, tunnels, VPNs, server changes, CI runs — ask first.
ai.sessionAccess.summary.custom: Custom: exactly what the {{group}} access group says.

It is hidden below until you ask for it. Copy the block below into an MCP client that speaks Streamable HTTP (e.g. Gemini CLI). Claude Desktop cannot use it — it ignores and and only launches stdio servers; use Overview → Connect Claude Desktop, which writes the bridge entry it does understand. For Claude Code, Overview → Connect Claude Code gives you a one-line command; Codex has .

ai.accessGroups.compareDesc: What each one allows, asks about, or refuses — read from the groups themselves.
ai.accessGroups.name: Name
ai.accessGroups.elevatedTitle: This group grants privileged access with no prompt
ai.accessGroups.elevatedDesc: An agent can act on it without you seeing anything. Set it to ASK in Capabilities below if you want to approve each use.
ai.accessGroups.confirmRiskyDesc: On: the actions below still ask even where a capability says Allow. Off: Allow means allow (a command whose program is computed at run time still asks unless Sudo is Allow). Applies to agents on the Custom profile using this group; the predefined profiles carry their own.
ai.accessGroups.capabilitiesHeading: Capabilities — set each of the {{count}} individually
ai.accessGroups.fileRulesDesc: The most specific matching pattern wins; anything unmatched falls back to Read/Write Files above. Sudo -i/su/bash-style unrestricted shells are blocked on every profile except Bypass, and are not configurable here.
ai.accessGroups.assignmentIntro: Nothing here is needed to give an agent access — a session's own access group is the grant, and a workspace with no assignment leaves it exactly as written. What an assignment does is hold a workspace below that grant, whatever group an agent was issued. A server with no override inherits its workspace's assignment.
ai.accessGroups.protectedIntro: Protected from agents is the other optional restriction, for production: every agent is held at Ask first there, whatever its profile; Read only stays read only.
ai.accessGroups.workspaceDefault: Default access group for this workspace
ai.accessGroups.workspaceDefaultDesc: A restriction narrows every profile except Bypass. To hold this target even against Bypass, mark it Protected. No AI Access holds for every profile.
ai.accessGroups.noRestriction: (no restriction — each session's own group applies)
ai.accessGroups.protectedDesc: Every agent is held at Ask first here, whatever its profile; Read only stays read only.
ai.accessGroups.createdNotOpen: Created {{name}}. It is not open yet — you have unsaved changes here.
ai.accessGroups.created: Created {{name}}. Read what its card says it allows before you assign it to anything.
ai.accessGroups.unavailable: OpsMaxx is not available in this window.
ai.accessGroups.deleted: Deleted {{name}}. Anything assigned to it is now No AI Access.
ai.accessGroups.notDeleted: {{name}} was not deleted: {{error}}. It may reappear when OpsMaxx restarts.
ai.accessGroups.intro: Access groups are for when the predefined profiles do not fit: an agent on the Custom profile does exactly what its group says, per capability, and a group assigned to a workspace or server restricts every agent there. Each card describes itself from its own settings. Pick one to change it, or create your own (Logs Only, Production Read Only, ...).
ai.accessGroups.unsavedDesc: The card shows them, but nothing is stored until you save — the policy engine is still enforcing the old settings. Opening {{name}} now discards them.
ai.accessGroups.nameNewDesc: A new group starts by allowing reads, asking before terminal and database access, refusing writes and sudo, and confirming risky actions. You can change all of it next.

operations.consequence.broadcast: Runs a shell command on every server you select.
operations.consequence.patch: Installs packages in waves, and restarts hosts that ask for it.
operations.consequence.jobs: Makes servers run things: once as a job, on a schedule, or as a service that survives you.
operations.consequence.keyRevoke: Removes one SSH key from every account across the estate that trusts it.
operations.consequence.cicdTrigger: Starts, cancels and disables builds on a CI server OpsMaxx does not administer, and cannot stop one once it runs.
operations.jobs.compose.label: Run a job
operations.jobs.compose.consequence: Runs multi-step work across servers in waves, with a rollback you press yourself.
operations.jobs.schedule.label: Change a schedule
operations.jobs.schedule.consequence: Replaces one server's crontab, after keeping a copy of it on that server.
operations.jobs.install.label: Install a service
operations.jobs.install.consequence: Writes a systemd --user unit onto one server and enables it.
operations.banner.sub: Everything here changes servers. Nothing here is a refresh.
operations.tabOff: {{name}} is switched off, so this is not it. {{detail}}
operations.empty.title: Nothing here can change a server yet.
operations.cron.scheduleNoReading: a schedule cron accepts — no plain-English reading of it is offered
operations.cron.scheduleInvalid: not a schedule cron accepts: five fields, or @reboot, @daily, @hourly and the rest
operations.cron.planFailed: the change could not be planned.
operations.cron.changed: Changed. The crontab as it was is on the server at {{path}}.
operations.cron.title: Change what a server runs on a schedule
operations.cron.about: Adds, changes or removes one job in the connected account’s own crontab, on one server. The whole file is replaced — that is the only way to write one — after a timestamped copy is kept on the server itself.
operations.cron.noBridge: This build’s main process has no crontab edit channels, so nothing here can write. Restart the app to rebuild it.
operations.cron.emptyBody: Pick a server and read it. A crontab is written back whole, so this reads the file it is about to replace first — a change planned against a file nobody read is a change that deletes the part nobody saw. The estate-wide view of what is scheduled, including the sources this account is not allowed to read, is on Monitoring.
operations.cron.unreadable: This account’s crontab on {{server}} was not read in full, so nothing here can be written to it. A write replaces the whole file, which means the part that could not be read is the part it would delete.
operations.cron.someUnreadable: Some other sources on this server were not readable; the list below is what was.
operations.cron.allRead: Every source on this server was read.
operations.cron.nothingFound: Nothing found in the sources that could be read.
operations.cron.replaceNote: The whole crontab is replaced — that is the only way to write one — after a timestamped copy of it is kept on {{server}}. It is written back only if the file is still the one this was planned against, and it is read back afterwards and compared; if it does not match, the copy goes straight back.
operations.cron.finalNewline: This crontab has no newline at the end of its last line, so one is being added. Without it the new job would be glued onto the end of the previous one.
operations.cron.reviewHint: Add or change a job above, then review it.
operations.revoke.outcome.revertedVerifi: Reverted — the server would not let a new session in
operations.revoke.outcome.revertedUnconf: Reverted — nothing confirmed it in time
operations.revoke.title: Revoke a key
operations.revoke.about: Removes one key from every account across the estate that trusts it. The inventory below is the reading the Monitoring sweep already took; nothing here re-reads a server until a change has been made to it.
operations.revoke.whySummary: Why it is off, and what it will be able to do
operations.revoke.emptyTitle: No keys have been collected to revoke.
operations.revoke.emptyBody: The authorized_keys sweep belongs to Fleet keys and access on Monitoring — this panel only acts on what that has already read, so with it switched off there is nothing here to act on. Nothing is revoked by reading, and nothing is read by opening this.
operations.revoke.unchecked_one: {{count}} server was not read, so this key may also be on it: {{servers}}. Revoking here removes it from the accounts listed below and from nowhere else.
operations.revoke.unchecked_other: {{count}} servers were not read, so this key may also be on them: {{servers}}. Revoking here removes it from the accounts listed below and from nowhere else.
operations.revoke.noLabelTitle: No comment on any line carrying this key. A key with no label is not an unused key — it is a key nobody wrote down the owner of.
operations.revoke.vaultReason: Revoking a key on these servers needs their stored credentials.
operations.revoke.confirmBody_one: This is staged, not applied. Each server takes a timestamped backup, replaces the file, and arms its OWN rollback before OpsMaxx lets go — so if this app dies in the next instant, the server puts the previous file back by itself after {{count}} second. Nothing becomes permanent until a second connection has authenticated against the changed file.
operations.revoke.confirmBody_other: This is staged, not applied. Each server takes a timestamped backup, replaces the file, and arms its OWN rollback before OpsMaxx lets go — so if this app dies in the next instant, the server puts the previous file back by itself after {{count}} seconds. Nothing becomes permanent until a second connection has authenticated against the changed file.

operations.revoke.leftOut_other: {{count}} left out, and not by choice:

operations.revoke.nothingRan: Nothing ran: every server was left out.

operations.revoke.gateBridge: Restart OpsMaxx to revoke keys — this window is newer than the process behind it.
operations.revoke.gateBuild: Changing authorized keys is not enabled in this build.
operations.revoke.chooseKeyTitle: Choose a key from the table above.

Install {{unit}} on {{server}}?

It writes ~/.config/systemd/user/{{unit}} and enables it. It does NOT start it, and any existing unit of that name is backed up first.

operations.unit.about: Writes a unit to ~/.config/systemd/user/ on one server and enables it. It is not started: the server’s own systemd owns it from then on, which is the point — it is there when OpsMaxx is not.

inspect.listening.sessions: Requests appear here as they happen. Terminals you open from now on are routed through the inspector automatically — ones that were already open are not.
inspect.listening.system: Requests appear here as they happen. This machine's proxy settings point at the inspector, so anything that honours them is captured.
inspect.listening.manual: Requests appear here as they happen. Nothing is pointed at the inspector automatically on this setting — use “Copy shell setup” to point a shell at it yourself.

inspect.detail.headersTruncated: The header list was longer than OpsMaxx records. The request itself was forwarded whole.
inspect.detail.upgraded: This connection was upgraded to another protocol after the handshake — a WebSocket, almost always. The handshake above is recorded; the frames that follow are not.
inspect.detail.binary: {{size}} of binary data ({{type}}). Not shown as text.
inspect.detail.truncated: This body was larger than the capture limit. It reached its destination in full; only the recording stops here.

processes.form.name: Name
processes.form.argumentsHelp: Separated by spaces, and passed straight to the program. There is no shell here, so nothing is expanded and nothing is quoted — and a secret in this list would be readable by every account on this machine through ps. Use an environment variable from the vault instead.
processes.form.secretHelp: A name that looks like a secret — anything with PASSWORD, TOKEN, SECRET, KEY or CREDENTIAL in it — can only come from the vault. The value is then read when the process starts, is never written to disk here, and is scrubbed out of the output below before it is stored.

processes.form.readyHelp: Plain text, matched anywhere in a line. Not a pattern language.

vault.reset.title: Delete this vault and start over
vault.reset.body: This deletes every entry in the vault and recovers nothing — the master password is the only thing that decrypts them, so there is no copy anywhere to fall back to. Your servers, databases, workspaces and settings stay exactly as they are, and so do the passwords and keys this machine keeps in its own keychain, so your connections keep working. What stops is anything that read its credential out of the vault — API tokens, CI tokens, VPN and process secrets — until you put it in the new one. Type DELETE to confirm.

vault.unlock.createIntro: There is no vault on this machine yet, so there is nowhere to keep this secret. The vault keeps passwords, SSH keys and other secrets encrypted here, so OpsMaxx can use them without you retyping them. Pick a master password to protect it — it is never stored anywhere, so if you lose it the contents cannot be recovered.

vault.gate.lockedBody: Enter the master password you chose for this vault. It stays open until you lock it, quit OpsMaxx, or your machine goes to sleep.
vault.gate.bioLater: You can turn on {{method}} unlock as soon as the vault is set up, so you mostly stop typing it — with the default setting you type it once each time OpsMaxx starts.
vault.gate.wrongPasswordHint: Master passwords are case sensitive — check caps lock. Nothing can recover one: only this password opens this vault. If it is gone for good, you can delete the vault and start over below.
vault.gate.wrongPasswordHintBio: Master passwords are case sensitive — check caps lock. Nothing can recover one: only this password opens this vault. If it is gone for good, you can delete the vault and start over below. You can also unlock with {{method}} above.
vault.bioOffer.title: Unlock with {{method}} next time?
vault.bioOffer.intro: Your master password is never stored either way, and you can change this at any time. Once it is on, opening a locked Vault asks for {{method}} on its own; cancel and the password field is still there. Settings turns that off.
vault.bioOffer.session: While the app is running — nothing extra is written to disk. You type the master password once per launch, and {{method}} reopens the vault after that.
vault.bioOffer.persistent: Across restarts — the vault’s key is saved to this Mac’s keychain, so you stop typing the password altogether. It is the more convenient choice and the weaker one: anything that can read that keychain entry as your account can then open the vault.

connections.cloud.azureAuthHint: Microsoft Entra ID. Azure issues a short-lived certificate for each connection; no key is stored and access expires on its own.

lib.capacity.refusal.whySparse: Samples are collected while OpsMaxx is running with background checking on, so leaving it running (Settings can start it at login, in the background) spreads them through the window.

lib.capacity.refusal.tooFewPoints_other: Only {{count}} samples so far; {{needed}} are needed over at least {{window}}.
lib.capacity.refusal.windowTooShort: Only {{held}} of data. A rate needs at least {{window}}, so that one backup or one build is not the whole trend.
lib.capacity.refusal.sparseUnknown: Samples cover too few parts of this window. A line through them would describe those hours rather than the window. {{advice}}
lib.capacity.refusal.sparse: Samples cover only {{occupied}} of {{parts}} parts of this window (the longest silence is {{gap}}). A line through them would describe those hours rather than the window. {{advice}}
lib.capacity.refusal.alreadyPast: Already at or over {{threshold}}%. There is nothing left to predict.
lib.capacity.refusal.flat: Flat over {{held}} — no measurable trend to project.
lib.capacity.refusal.noisy: This {{label}} moves too much between samples for a trend line to mean anything.
lib.capacity.refusal.stepChange: The rise over {{held}} is one step, not a trend — something was written once. A forecast from it would be about that event, not about the {{label}}.
lib.capacity.refusal.beyondHorizon: More than {{days}} days out at this rate, which is further ahead than this will guess.
lib.capacity.forecast.withinDay: Reaches {{threshold}}% within a day — {{date}} — from {{held}} of data.
lib.capacity.forecast.withinDayCovered: Reaches {{threshold}}% within a day — {{date}} — from {{held}} of data ({{occupied}}/{{parts}} parts sampled).
lib.capacity.forecast.inSpanCovered: Reaches {{threshold}}% in {{span}} — {{date}} — from {{held}} of data ({{occupied}}/{{parts}} parts sampled).
lib.capacity.confidence.high: The points sit close to the line and there are several days of them.
lib.capacity.confidence.medium: The line fits reasonably, over at least a day.
lib.capacity.confidence.low: A short run, or a loose fit. Treat the date as a hint, not a plan.

lib.ruleReach.webhookOff: Webhook delivery is switched off, so this rule will match and send nothing. Turn it on in Settings → Alerts.

vpn.profileForm.systemModeBlocked: System mode is not available on macOS: OpsMaxx has no signed privileged helper, so it cannot create a system network interface. Userspace mode gives the same tunnel through local listeners and needs no administrator rights.
vpn.profileForm.modeUserspaceHint: The tunnel is exposed as local listeners only. No TUN device, no route changes, no elevation prompt.
vpn.profileForm.modeSystemHint: Creates a real network interface and changes routes and DNS. Asks for elevation every time it starts. A full tunnel (0.0.0.0/0) is not supported in this mode.

vpn.profileForm.stillUsesNoKey: Until you do, this profile still uses no key at all.
vpn.profileForm.pendingReplaces: This key replaces the stored one when you press Save.
vpn.profileForm.pendingSaves: This key is saved to the vault when you press Save.
vpn.profileForm.publicKeyHint: Give this to your VPN provider, or add it to your server’s [Peer] section. It is not a secret — the private key above is.
vpn.profileForm.keyHintCannotMint: This build cannot generate keys. Import a .conf that already carries one.
vpn.profileForm.keyHintDirty: Nothing is written to the vault until you say so.
vpn.profileForm.keyHintPending: The private key goes to the vault on Save, and never onto this profile, a config file, or a log line.
vpn.profileForm.keyHintInVault: Private key, held in the vault. OpsMaxx cannot read it back to show you its public key — paste the key here to see it, or generate a new pair and authorise that one instead.
vpn.profileForm.keyHintNone: No private key yet. Generate a pair, or paste one you already have; either way it goes to the vault on Save and the profile keeps only a pointer to it.
vpn.profileForm.listenersHint: In userspace mode these are the only way traffic reaches the tunnel — nothing is routed system-wide.
vpn.profileForm.authUserpassOtp: Username, password and a one-time code
vpn.profileForm.tailscaleIntro: OpsMaxx joins your tailnet itself — there is nothing to install. This profile is its own device, with its own key, so it neither uses nor disturbs a Tailscale app you may also be running on this machine.
vpn.profileForm.deviceNameSharedHint: How this appears in your tailnet's device list. Letters, digits and dashes. This one is part of the profile, so it travels to every computer you have paired — and a tailnet name identifies a single device, so if two of them run this profile Tailscale keeps them apart by adding -1, -2. Give the second computer a name of its own below.
vpn.profileForm.deviceNameLocalHint: Overrides the name above, here and nowhere else. It is stored with this node's key on this machine and never syncs, so setting it does not rename anybody else's device. Leave it empty to use the profile's name.
vpn.profileForm.appearsAsOverridden: This computer will appear as {{name}} — the name above is unchanged elsewhere.
vpn.profileForm.noDeviceName: No name set, so Tailscale will choose one for this computer.
vpn.profileForm.showPeersHint: List the devices on this tailnet. Read-only — it changes what OpsMaxx shows, never the tailnet itself. Off by default, because a device list is information about a network you may not want mirrored here.
vpn.profileForm.openvpnCredentialsHint: Credentials live in the vault and are handed to OpenVPN over its management socket — never written to a file, never passed on the command line.
vpn.profileForm.redirectGateway: Send all traffic through this VPN. Off by default: a downloaded profile asking for your default route is not a good enough reason to give it.
vpn.profileForm.binaryHintUserSupplied: OpsMaxx does not ship OpenVPN on this platform. Leave this empty to use an allowlisted system install.
vpn.profileForm.binaryHintBundled: OpsMaxx ships an OpenVPN and uses it by default. Set a path only to run a copy you installed yourself.
vpn.profileForm.binaryHintUnknown: Leave this empty to use the OpenVPN OpsMaxx finds by itself.
vpn.profileForm.tlsEnable: Encrypt the control connection with TLS
vpn.profileForm.plaintextConfirm: Send the control connection unencrypted. Anyone on the path can read the token and the traffic.

vpn.profileForm.noProxies: An frp client with no proxies connects and exposes nothing.

k8s.panel.execNoTty: One command, no TTY and no stdin: a program that waits for input will hang until the timeout rather than prompt. This is not a shell session.
k8s.panel.watching: Watching this cluster for restarting pods. Checked every two minutes from {{server}}. An alert is raised when a pod’s restart count goes up between checks — a count on its own cannot tell a pod that is restarting now from one that restarted last week.

shared.access.statusHelp.ok: Read successfully. An empty list here means empty, not "we could not look".
shared.access.statusHelp.partial: Some of it was read and some was not. The values shown are real; they are not the whole picture, and the accounts that could not be read are counted separately rather than being left out.
shared.access.statusHelp.absent: This server does not have the file that answers this, and that was checked rather than assumed.
shared.access.statusHelp.denied: It exists and this account was not allowed to read it. A different account, or passwordless sudo, would see more. This is NOT the same as there being nothing there.
shared.access.statusHelp.noTool: The program that answers this is not installed on this server.
shared.access.statusHelp.unsupported: This server cannot answer this question at all — not a permission problem and not a missing tool. Treat it as UNKNOWN, never as "none".
shared.access.statusHelp.unknown: The probe ran and its answer could not be read, or the collector never reported on it.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.malformed: This line is in the file and is not a key OpsMaxx can read. sshd may still accept it, so it is counted rather than hidden.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.unknownType: The key type on this line is not one this version of OpsMaxx knows. It is very likely valid — a newer algorithm — and it is NOT fingerprinted, so it will not match anything in the fleet view.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.badBase64: The key body on this line is not valid base64, so no fingerprint could be computed from it.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.typeMismatc: The algorithm named at the start of the line is not the algorithm inside the key itself. sshd rejects lines like this; a person reading the file would not notice.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.truncated: This line was longer than the collector transmits and arrived cut short, so its fingerprint would be wrong. The line is reported and deliberately not fingerprinted.
shared.access.keyProblemHelp.certificate: This line trusts a certificate, and the public key inside the certificate could not be read out of it. The certificate itself is deliberately not fingerprinted: that value is different for every certificate issued to the same key, so it would match nothing on any other server while looking like an answer.
shared.access.source.notReported: the collector did not report on this source
shared.access.uncertainty.accountsUnread: {{unread}} of {{total}} accounts could not be read, so any key they trust is not counted here
shared.access.uncertainty.authorizedKeys: sshd is configured with an AuthorizedKeysCommand, so it can accept keys that are not in any file on disk
shared.access.uncertainty.keyFileNotDefa: sshd is configured to read authorized keys from a path other than the default, which this collection does not read
shared.access.uncertainty.keyFileUnknown: sshd’s AuthorizedKeysFile setting could not be determined, so it is not known whether this is where it looks
shared.access.uncertainty.otherKeyFile: sshd does not read .ssh/authorized_keys on this server, which is the file this collection read, so the keys listed here are not the keys it accepts

shared.access.write.optInNote: Adding and revoking keys is off by default. Every refusal and both rollbacks are built and tested, and the change is staged behind a dead-man’s switch on the server itself — but nobody has yet watched that switch fire on a real RHEL 9 server with KillUserProcesses=yes, which is the case it exists for. Turn this on only if you can afford to be locked out of the server you point it at, and keep a second session open while you try it.
shared.access.write.disabledSummary: Changing authorized keys is not enabled in this build. Reading is unaffected — nothing on this screen writes to any server.
shared.access.write.offSummary: Revoking keys is switched off. Turn on “Allow adding and revoking keys on servers” in Settings to use it. Nothing on this screen writes to any server until you do.
shared.access.write.staleBridge: Restart OpsMaxx to revoke keys — this window is newer than the process behind it. Reading is unaffected.
shared.access.write.disabledReason: Changing authorized keys is not enabled in this build. The safety net behind it — the server restoring its own previous file if nothing confirms the change — is not yet dependable, and a rollback that cannot be relied on is worse than no rollback at all, because it tells you that you are safe. Reading is unaffected: nothing on this screen writes to any server.
shared.access.write.scope: Even once it is enabled it will only ever edit ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for the account OpsMaxx connects as on each server — not another account’s file, and not any path sshd was configured to read instead. On the account it connects as it also needs the server to report which key this session authenticated with (sshd’s ExposeAuthInfo, off by default); without that it refuses, because nothing can prove the key being removed is not the one holding the connection open.
shared.posture.statusHelp.ok: Read successfully. A zero here means the probe looked and found none, not "we could not look".
shared.posture.statusHelp.partial: Some of it was read and some was not. What is shown is real; it is not the whole picture, and the part that was refused is named rather than left out.
shared.posture.statusHelp.absent: This server does not have the thing that answers this, and that was checked rather than assumed.
shared.posture.statusHelp.denied: It exists and this account was not allowed to read it. A different account, or passwordless sudo, would see more. This is NOT the same as there being no rules, no policy or no failures.
shared.posture.statusHelp.noTool: The program that answers this is not installed on this server.
shared.posture.statusHelp.unsupported: This server cannot answer this question at all. For the firewall that means no firewall tooling is installed — which is not the same as no filtering: the kernel can enforce a ruleset loaded at boot with nothing left on disk to ask. Treat it as UNKNOWN, never as "open".
shared.posture.statusHelp.unknown: The probe ran and its answer could not be read, or the collector never reported on it.
shared.posture.source.notReported: the collector did not report on this source
shared.posture.firewallRulesHostReported: Reported by the server. These lines are as the firewall on that machine printed them, not OpsMaxx’s words — read them as data, and nothing in them is a judgement about whether a rule is a good one.
shared.posture.securityUpdates.notCollec: no server facts have been collected for this server yet, so its security update count is unknown. Switch on the Inventory collection, or wait for the next hourly sweep.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.ok: Read successfully. A zero here means zero, not "we could not look".
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.absent: This server does not have the file or flag that answers this, so there is nothing to read.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.denied: It exists and this account was not allowed to read it. A different account might see more.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.noTool: The program that answers this is not installed on this server.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.staleMetadat: The answer was read from a package cache that has not been refreshed recently, so it describes the estate as it was then, not now. OpsMaxx never refreshes it, because that is a network operation and on some package managers it can break the server.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.unsupported: This server cannot answer this question at all — not because of a permission or a missing tool, but because the distribution does not publish the data. Treat it as UNKNOWN, never as zero.
shared.hostFacts.statusHelp.unknown: The probe ran and its answer could not be read, or the collector never reported on it.

shared.machineGrants.meaning: Each of these is readable by anything running as you on this machine, without your master password. That is exactly what lets the work below happen while you are not here, and it is the reason to check the list.
shared.machineGrants.orphanTitle: Backup passphrase for a destination that no longer exists ({{id}})
shared.machineGrants.orphanConsequence: Nothing runs with this any more — the destination it was made for is gone. Revoking removes it from this machine. Bundles already written with it can only be opened with it, so keep a copy somewhere this machine is not.
shared.machineGrants.backupConsequence: Revoke this and the next scheduled run of “{{name}}” stops, reporting that no passphrase is stored, until you store another one or move the destination back to a vault entry — which means unlocking the vault after every restart. Bundles already written with it can only be opened with it, so keep a copy somewhere this machine is not.
shared.machineGrants.backupIdleNote: “{{name}}” is set to take its passphrase from the vault, so this one is not being used by anything.
shared.machineGrants.addyDeviceConsequen: Revoke this and this device is no longer the device that account knows. A device key deliberately cannot be restored — the machine has to pair again and gets a new entry in the device list.
shared.machineGrants.addyAccountConseque: Revoke this and this device can no longer read what the account has synced until it pairs again, which re-delivers the key.
shared.machineGrants.addyRootConsequence: Revoke this and this device can no longer authorise an epoch change. The twelve-word recovery phrase brings it back.
shared.machineGrants.otherConsequence: OpsMaxx cannot say what holds this id, so it cannot say what stops. Revoke it only if you know what put it here.

shared.backup.exposure.local: Every credential in this app, your vault and your trusted host keys will be written to this directory as an encrypted file. Anyone who can read the directory and guess the passphrase has all of it. A synced folder (Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud) copies it onward.
shared.backup.exposure.sftp: Every credential in this app, your vault and your trusted host keys will be uploaded to this server as an encrypted file. Anyone with an account there that can read the directory holds your secrets, offline, for as long as the file exists.
shared.backup.exposure.s3: Every credential in this app, your vault and your trusted host keys will be uploaded to this bucket as an encrypted file. A bucket that is public, or whose keys leak, hands over the whole file — the passphrase is then the only thing left between someone and your estate.
shared.backup.exposure.addy: Every credential in this app, your vault and your trusted host keys will be uploaded to your relay as an encrypted file, sealed a second time under your account key — so the relay itself cannot read it even with the passphrase. Someone who holds one of your enrolled devices and the passphrase has all of it.
shared.backup.s3Prefix.emptySegment: The key prefix “{{prefix}}” has an empty path segment. Object stores reject a key with “//” in it, so nothing would ever be written here.
shared.backup.s3Prefix.dotSegment: The key prefix “{{prefix}}” has a “{{segment}}” path segment. The request is signed over the path before the URL is parsed, and the parser removes that segment afterwards — so the store would answer SignatureDoesNotMatch and it would look like the access key was wrong.

shared.backup.problem.passphraseEntry: A scheduled run has nobody to type a passphrase, so it needs a vault entry holding one.

Treat it like the API key it stands in for, and rotate it when you would have rotated that.
shared.credproxy.loopbackNote: Every process on this machine can reach a loopback port, so being local is not a permission. The token is what separates your script from anything else running as you.
