shared.drift.statusHelp.ok: Read in full and compared. A verdict of "identical" here means identical, not "we could not look".
shared.drift.statusHelp.partial: The file is larger than the read cap, so only the beginning could be read — and a comparison over the beginning would call two files with different endings the same. It is reported, and not compared.
shared.drift.statusHelp.absent: This server does not have the file, and that was checked rather than inferred from a failed stat.
shared.drift.statusHelp.denied: It exists and this account was not allowed to read it, or the directory above it could not be traversed. This is NOT the same as the file being absent, and it is NOT the same as matching.
shared.drift.statusHelp.noTool: The server has no base64, so the collector had no safe way to carry the content back.
shared.drift.statusHelp.unsupported: The path exists and is not a regular file. There is nothing here to compare.
shared.drift.statusHelp.unknown: The probe ran and this file was not reported on, or its content arrived cut off. Treat as UNKNOWN — never as "none" and never as "the same as everyone else".
shared.drift.rule.lineEndings.label: Line endings
shared.drift.rule.lineEndings.detail: Treats a CRLF line ending as a LF one. A file edited on Windows and the same file edited on the server are the same file.
shared.drift.rule.includeLines.label: Include directives
shared.drift.rule.includeLines.detail: Drops whole lines whose first word is include, Include, include_dir, includedir or .include. These point at per-server drop-in directories, so they differ by design — and dropping them means the CONTENT of those drop-ins is not compared either, because this reads one path per server.
shared.drift.rule.comments.label: Whole-line comments
shared.drift.rule.comments.detail: Drops lines whose first non-blank character is the watched file's comment character. Only WHOLE-line comments: a trailing comment after a directive is left alone, because deciding where a comment starts inside a line means knowing the file's quoting rules, and getting that wrong silently changes a directive.
shared.drift.rule.timestamps.label: Dates and times
shared.drift.rule.timestamps.detail: Replaces ISO dates, ISO date-times, bare HH:MM:SS clock times and ten-digit unix seconds with a placeholder. This is what a "generated at" header churns on. It also hides a genuine difference between two dates that are both dates — a certificate validity line, for instance — so it is off for files where a date is the setting.
shared.drift.rule.hostnames.label: The server's own name
shared.drift.rule.hostnames.detail: Replaces this server's hostname, its short name and the server's name in OpsMaxx with a placeholder, case-insensitively. A template that stamps the machine's name into a file makes every copy unique; this is what makes them comparable. It cannot see a per-server name it was not told about.
shared.drift.rule.trailingSpace.label: Trailing whitespace
shared.drift.rule.trailingSpace.detail: Removes spaces and tabs at the end of a line. Nothing reads them and every editor treats them differently.
shared.drift.rule.innerSpace.label: Runs of spaces inside a line
shared.drift.rule.innerSpace.detail: Collapses a run of spaces or tabs BETWEEN two tokens down to one space. Leading indentation is left exactly as it is, because in a YAML file indentation is the syntax.
shared.drift.rule.blankLines.label: Blank lines
shared.drift.rule.blankLines.detail: Drops lines that are empty or contain only whitespace. A file's final newline is its terminator rather than a blank line, so whether a file ends with one stops being a difference — and this rule does not report itself as having done work merely because a file ended properly.
shared.drift.rule.lineOrder.label: Line order
shared.drift.rule.lineOrder.detail: Sorts the remaining lines, so two files with the same lines in a different order compare equal. The loudest rule here: in a file where order is meaning — an nginx location block, an iptables ruleset — this will call two genuinely different configurations the same. It is off unless the watched file is a set rather than a sequence.
shared.drift.rule.unknown.detail: This version of OpsMaxx does not know what this rule does, so it is not applied.
shared.drift.watch.sshdConfig.label: sshd configuration
shared.drift.watch.sshdConfig.note: Include lines are dropped because a drop-in directory is per-server by design. Order is NOT normalised: in sshd_config the first occurrence of a keyword wins, so two files with the same lines in a different order are two different configurations.
shared.drift.watch.nginxConf.note: Hostnames are substituted because server_name is templated per server. Order is not normalised: location matching is ordered.
shared.drift.watch.resolvConf.note: Order is not normalised: nameserver lines are tried in the order they appear, so a server that lists the secondary first is genuinely different.
shared.drift.watch.hosts.note: The one watch with line-order on: /etc/hosts is a lookup table, not a sequence, and every server has its own name in it — which the hostnames rule substitutes so the tables can be compared at all.
shared.drift.watch.sysctlConf.note: Order is normalised: sysctl.conf is a set of key = value settings and the last assignment wins, so two files with the same assignments in a different order do apply the same kernel settings.
shared.drift.watch.chronyConf.note: Time sources drifting apart across a fleet is the classic cause of "the logs do not line up". Order is not normalised: chrony tries sources in order.
shared.drift.watch.timezone.note: One line. Almost nothing is normalised because there is almost nothing to normalise, which makes it the cheapest illustration of what a clean comparison looks like.
shared.drift.verdict.notCollected: this server has not been collected yet
shared.drift.coverage.denied: {{hosts}} would not let this account read it — that is not the same as matching
shared.drift.coverage.unsupported: the path is not a regular file on {{hosts}}
shared.drift.coverage.redacted: secret-shaped text was replaced before comparing on {{hosts}}, so a difference inside it is invisible here
shared.drift.noPush: Configuration drift reads and compares. It never writes a file to a server to bring it into line: that is a job, and it goes through a plan you read and an approval minted against it, not a button on a comparison. Nor could this panel decide which side is right — a server that was fixed first and a server that drifted look the same from here.
shared.logtail.source.noTarget: Give a unit name or a log file path.
shared.logtail.source.since: That is not a time journalctl will take. Try "2 hours ago", "yesterday" or "2024-01-01 09:30".
shared.logtail.source.containerRef: That is not a container name or id.
shared.logtail.source.containerFilters: Priority and since are journald filters and do not apply to a container.
shared.logtail.source.unitName: That is not a unit name. Letters, digits and - _ . @ : only.
shared.logtail.source.relativePath: Use an absolute path, starting with /.
shared.logtail.source.pathChars: That path contains characters this will not pass to a shell.
shared.logtail.issue.noJournal: No journalctl on this server, so it is not running systemd — Alpine, a container, or a pre-systemd distribution. Switch to File and give a path such as /var/log/messages.
shared.logtail.issue.noTail: No tail on the PATH an SSH session gets, which is unusual enough to be worth checking by hand.
shared.logtail.issue.unitNotLoaded: systemd does not know this unit. Check the name: journalctl will follow a unit that does not exist and show you nothing at all.
shared.logtail.issue.unitMasked: This unit is masked, so it cannot run and will not be logging.
shared.logtail.issue.journalUnreadable: The journal returned nothing for this unit and this account is not root, nor in systemd-journal, adm or wheel. An empty pane here does NOT mean the service is quiet — it means you are not being shown what it said.
shared.logtail.issue.unitQuiet: The unit exists and its journal is readable, so it genuinely has not logged anything in this window.
shared.logtail.issue.fileMissing: That path does not exist yet. tail -F keeps waiting and picks the file up the moment it appears — right when you are watching for a log about to be written, and an empty pane forever otherwise.
shared.logtail.issue.fileDenied: That file exists but this account cannot read it. /var/log/secure and /var/log/audit/audit.log are root-only on most servers.
shared.logtail.issue.fileIsDir: That path is a directory, not a file.
shared.logtail.issue.noDocker: No docker on this server. Looked on PATH and in the usual install directories — if it lives somewhere else, a symlink into /usr/local/bin is the usual fix.
shared.logtail.issue.dockerDenied: This account cannot reach the docker socket, so it cannot read container logs. Adding it to the docker group grants root-equivalent access on most installs, which is a decision worth making deliberately.
shared.logtail.issue.containerMissing: No container with that name or id on this server. It may have been removed, or the name may belong to a different server.
shared.logtail.issue.containerStopped: That container is not running. Its logs are still readable — this is history, not a live stream, and nothing new will arrive until it starts again.
shared.localMounts.mountpoint.empty: Choose where to mount it on the server.
shared.localMounts.mountpoint.padded: The mount point starts or ends with a space.
shared.localMounts.mountpoint.controlCha: The mount point has a control character in it.
shared.localMounts.mountpoint.tooLong: The mount point is too long.
shared.localMounts.mountpoint.rootOrHome: Mount into a folder of its own, not over the root or your home folder.
shared.localMounts.failure.noSshfs: sshfs is not installed on this server.
shared.localMounts.failure.noSshfsFix: Install it on the server: {{apt}} (Debian, Ubuntu) or {{dnf}} (Fedora, RHEL).
shared.localMounts.failure.noFuse: /dev/fuse is not available on this server.
shared.localMounts.failure.noFuseFix: Containers usually lack it. On a full machine, load the module with {{command}}.
shared.localMounts.failure.fuseDenied: {{user}} is not allowed to use /dev/fuse on this server.
shared.localMounts.failure.fuseDeniedNoU: This account is not allowed to use /dev/fuse on this server.
shared.localMounts.failure.fuseDeniedFix: Where /dev/fuse belongs to a fuse group (some older or hardened systems; not Ubuntu or Debian), add the account on the server: {{command}}. Then press Retry: it opens a new connection, which is what picks up the new group.
shared.localMounts.failure.notEmpty: The mount point already has files in it.
shared.localMounts.failure.notEmptyFix: Mounting over them would hide them. Choose an empty or new folder.
shared.localMounts.failure.mkdir: Could not create the mount point on the server. {{said}}
shared.localMounts.failure.refused: The server refused the FUSE mount.
shared.localMounts.failure.refusedFix: This is what happens inside most containers, which cannot mount filesystems.
shared.changelog.sourceScope.localShell: which shells started and how they exited — never keystrokes, and never what a shell printed.
shared.changelog.sourceScope.approvals: what a human was asked before a job or a broadcast ran, and what they answered, with the commands as they were confirmed.
shared.changelog.sourceScope.agentAudit: what an agent did through the MCP bridge. This is the one source here that is not yours, and it is shown so the timeline is not missing the half you did not do.
shared.changelog.sourceScope.history: alerts raised and resolved, jobs, and what the durable store did about its own retention. Job output is deliberately not read.
shared.changelog.state.read: Read in full for this window.
shared.changelog.state.off: Not read: the change log is switched off, so this source was not opened.
shared.changelog.state.absent: Nothing to read yet — this record does not exist on this machine. That is not the same as a quiet week, and it is shown rather than left as an empty stretch of timeline.
shared.changelog.state.unreadable: Could NOT be read, so anything it holds is missing from the timeline below.
shared.changelog.state.truncated: Only the most recent part was read. Older entries exist and are NOT in the timeline below.
shared.changelog.state.partial: Read, except for lines that would not parse. Those were skipped; everything either side of them is here.
shared.changelog.coverage.rowsDropped_on: {{count}} older entry was past this page's budget for one source.
shared.changelog.coverage.rowsDropped_ot: {{count}} older entries were past this page's budget for one source.
shared.changelog.switchOn: The change log reads four records that already exist and merges them into one timeline. It stores nothing of its own and writes nothing.
shared.changelog.switchOff: The change log is off, so nothing is read and no timeline is assembled. This does NOT stop anything being recorded: the agent audit log, the local session log, the approval log and the durable store all go on writing exactly as before, because each is relied on by something other than this view. Switching this off removes the timeline, not the records behind it.
shared.mcp.mode.readOnly.label: Read only
shared.mcp.mode.ask.label: Ask first
shared.mcp.mode.ask.detail: Approve every change before it runs
shared.mcp.mode.auto.label: Auto
shared.mcp.mode.auto.detail: Routine work runs; sudo and risky actions ask
shared.mcp.mode.bypass.label: Bypass permissions
shared.mcp.mode.bypass.detail: No prompts or blocks, except on Protected targets
shared.mcp.mode.custom.detail: Use an access group, exactly as written
shared.mcp.capability.viewServer.label: View server
shared.mcp.capability.viewServer.detail: Lets an agent see that this server exists and read the permissions it has on it. Hostnames, usernames and keys are never disclosed.
shared.mcp.capability.terminal.label: Execute terminal commands
shared.mcp.capability.terminal.detail: Runs shell commands over SSH. Unrestricted privilege-escalation shells (sudo -i, su, sudo bash) are refused whatever this is set to, in every mode but Bypass. While the group's Confirm risky actions is on, a destructive, elevated or run-time-computed command still asks even when this is allow. It also governs pod_command, one command run inside a Kubernetes container, which is checked against the same command rules and asked for on every call even when this is allow (only the Bypass profile skips it).
shared.mcp.capability.readFiles.label: Read files
shared.mcp.capability.readFiles.detail: Reads file contents and lists directories. The path rules below can widen or narrow this per path.
shared.mcp.capability.writeFiles.label: Write files
shared.mcp.capability.writeFiles.detail: Creates, overwrites, renames and deletes files, and creates directories. The path rules below can widen or narrow this per path.
shared.mcp.capability.sftpDownload.label: SFTP download
shared.mcp.capability.sftpDownload.detai: The transport underneath reading. Applied on top of the path rules, so denying it blocks every path regardless of what they say.
shared.mcp.capability.sftpUpload.label: SFTP upload
shared.mcp.capability.sftpUpload.detail: The transport underneath writing. Denying it blocks every path regardless of what the rules say.
shared.mcp.capability.sshTunnel.label: SSH tunnels
shared.mcp.capability.sshTunnel.detail: Lists tunnels, defines and removes them, and opens or closes a forward. A local forward and a SOCKS proxy listen on this machine; a remote forward listens on the SERVER, where a non-loopback address publishes the port to that server’s network. Defining one does not start it. While the group's Confirm risky actions is on, defining, removing and opening all ask even when this is allow.
shared.mcp.capability.databaseAccess.det: Lists databases and runs queries against them through the server.
shared.mcp.capability.sudo.label: Sudo / privilege escalation
shared.mcp.capability.sudo.detail: Commands beginning with sudo, checked on top of Execute terminal commands. Path rules still apply — sudo does not waive them.
shared.mcp.capability.serverMetrics.deta: CPU, memory, disk and uptime — and also every failed systemd unit and every listening port with the process that owns it. That is a service and port inventory of the server, not only its capacity.
shared.mcp.capability.hostFacts.label: Host inventory & pending security updates
shared.mcp.capability.hostFacts.detail: Distribution and version, CPU model, architecture, virtualisation type, package manager, how many updates are pending, how many of those are SECURITY updates, and whether the server is waiting on a reboot. That is a patch-status report: it tells an agent which of your servers are unpatched and against what.
shared.mcp.capability.firewallRules.labe: Firewall rules: the addresses and ports this server accepts
shared.mcp.capability.firewallRules.deta: The rule lines themselves, as ufw, firewalld, nft or iptables print them — every address, port and protocol named in them, capped and stripped of control characters on the server. That is an inventory of what this server is exposed on and to whom, which is the thing an attacker would otherwise have to scan for. No agent can read it whatever this is set to: it is not behind any MCP tool. Setting it to allow lets OpsMaxx COLLECT the rules for this server, for a person to read in Security posture; anything else and they are never asked for.
shared.mcp.capability.sudoersRead.label: Sudoers: who can become root on this server
shared.mcp.capability.sudoersRead.detail: The rules in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d — which accounts and groups may run which commands as root, and which of them need no password. OpsMaxx reads it to replace a guess it makes today, that anyone in wheel or sudo has root, which is wrong in both directions. It is also the shortest description of how to take this machine, so it is asked for separately and never by an agent: no MCP tool exposes it whatever this is set to. Setting it to allow lets OpsMaxx COLLECT it for a person to read in Keys and access; anything else and it is never asked for.
shared.mcp.capability.manageServers.labe: Add, change and remove servers and databases in the workspace
shared.mcp.capability.manageServers.deta: Adds a server to the workspace, changes a saved one — including where it points, which account it uses and which other saved server it jumps through — and removes one. It does not grant any access to the servers it manages. While the group's Confirm risky actions is on, adding is the only part allow makes silent: changing and removing an existing connection still ask. When a change asks, approving it covers further changes to that same server for the rest of that agent session and nothing else; each removal is asked for on its own. With Confirm risky actions off, allow is a standing permission to repoint or delete what is already saved. The same applies to saved database connections, including which saved server a database is reached through; querying a database is Database access, not this.
shared.mcp.capability.vpnControl.label: VPN & reverse proxies
shared.mcp.capability.vpnControl.detail: Lists VPN profiles and reverse proxies, and starts or stops the VPNs. While the group's Confirm risky actions is on, starting a VPN, or stopping one live sessions depend on, asks even when this is allow. Reverse proxies are refused to an agent whatever this is set to; only a session you have put in Bypass mode can start or stop one.
shared.mcp.capability.containers.label: Containers and Kubernetes: what is running, and their logs
shared.mcp.capability.containers.detail: Lists containers with their image, state, ports, uptime and compose project, and reads container logs. The logs are the part to weigh: an application writes its own connection strings, tokens and customer records to stdout, and this returns them as the container emitted them. It reads only — starting and stopping is a separate permission. It also covers the Kubernetes cluster a server's kubeconfig reaches: pods, workloads, nodes, events, pod logs, Helm releases, and which secrets exist and who is bound to what (names only, never a secret's value — but together a map of how to escalate).
shared.mcp.capability.containerControl.l: Containers and Kubernetes: start, stop, restart and drain
shared.mcp.capability.containerControl.d: Restarts, stops and starts containers, and brings compose projects up and down. Stopping a container is an outage for whatever it serves, so this is separate from reading the list: an agent that may see what is running does not thereby get to stop it. In Kubernetes it covers a rolling restart of one workload and cordoning, uncordoning or draining one node; each is asked for on every call even when this is allow (only the Bypass profile skips it), and a drain refuses whenever its own preflight finds a blocker.
shared.mcp.capability.backupRead.label: Backups: whether they are running and when they last succeeded
shared.mcp.capability.backupRead.detail: Reads the backup destinations and how each is doing — the last successful run, how late it is, and any alarm raised against it. It names destinations and their kind, never their credentials. Running a backup and restoring one are not here at any setting: a run outlives the approval that started it, and a restore overwrites data.
shared.mcp.capability.fleetRead.label: Fleet: read across many servers at once
shared.mcp.capability.fleetRead.detail: Answers questions over everything already collected rather than one host at a time — the inventory, search across it, drift, alerts and the running process list. One call can return data from every server in the workspace, so the reach is the workspace and not the server this is set on.
shared.mcp.capability.ciRead.label: CI/CD: pipelines, runs and build output
shared.mcp.capability.ciRead.detail: Lists the CI connections, the pipelines on them and their recent runs, and reads the output a run produced. The output is the part to weigh, the same way container logs are: a build prints whatever its steps echo — access tokens, deploy keys, the contents of a test fixture — and this returns it as the runner recorded it. It is also written by whoever opened the merge request that ran it, so it is the least trustworthy text the bridge can hand an agent.
shared.mcp.capability.ciTrigger.label: CI/CD: start, cancel and re-run pipelines
shared.mcp.capability.ciTrigger.detail: Starts a pipeline run on the CI server, cancels one, or re-runs it. What that run then does is defined on the provider and not here: OpsMaxx cannot read the pipeline definition before it starts, and cannot see what it deploys or where. Stopping AI access takes away the agent's cancel along with everything else, so a run already accepted is then yours to stop — from the Stop button on that run in CI/CD, or in the provider. While the group's Confirm risky actions is on, starting, cancelling and re-running ask even when this is allow, and one approval never covers the next call; with it off in Auto mode, or in a Bypass session, a build starts unasked — except on a Protected workspace, and Ask first always asks.
shared.mcp.riskyAction.destructiveComman: destructive or elevated commands (rm -rf, mkfs, reboot, package installs, service restarts) — a destructive one also asks with the switch off unless Write files is Allow, and stopping or removing containers unless Container control is Allow
shared.mcp.riskyAction.computedCommands: commands whose program is computed at run time (these also ask with the switch off, unless Sudo is Allow), and unshare -r
shared.mcp.riskyAction.sshTunnels: opening, defining or deleting SSH tunnels
shared.mcp.riskyAction.vpn: starting a VPN, or stopping one other sessions depend on
shared.mcp.riskyAction.ciPipelines: starting, cancelling or re-running CI/CD pipelines
shared.approvalRisk.reason.sudo: the command runs as root, through sudo
shared.approvalRisk.reason.shell: it runs a shell command of the agent’s own composition on the host
shared.approvalRisk.reason.writeFiles: it overwrites a file on the host, and the previous contents are not kept anywhere
shared.approvalRisk.reason.databaseWrite: the statement was not classified as a read, so OpsMaxx is treating it as one that changes data
shared.approvalRisk.reason.databaseRead: it reads from a database through the host
shared.approvalRisk.reason.hostFacts: it returns which security updates the host is missing, which is what the host is unpatched against
shared.approvalRisk.reason.serverMetrics: it returns the host’s listening ports and failed services, not only its CPU and memory
shared.approvalRisk.reason.tunnelDefine: it writes a tunnel into OpsMaxx that outlives this session, and whoever presses Start next starts it
shared.approvalRisk.reason.tunnelRemove: it deletes a saved tunnel, and anything that expected that port loses it
shared.approvalRisk.reason.tunnelOpen: it opens a network path between this machine and a port on the server
shared.approvalRisk.reason.tunnelClose: it closes a tunnel that other things may still be using
shared.approvalRisk.reason.vpnStart: it changes which network your later SSH and database sessions travel over
shared.approvalRisk.reason.vpnStop: it stops a VPN that other sessions may depend on
shared.approvalRisk.reason.serverRemove: it deletes a saved connection and its stored credential, and OpsMaxx keeps no copy to put back
shared.approvalRisk.reason.serverChange: it rewrites a saved connection — where it points, which account it uses, or what it jumps through
shared.approvalRisk.reason.serverAdd: it writes to OpsMaxx’s own connection list and stores a credential there
shared.approvalRisk.whereWorkspace: Workspace: {{workspace}} — the whole workspace, no single server
shared.approvalRisk.unrecorded: OpsMaxx did not record why this scored {{level}}, and cannot derive it from the request. Judge it from the command below, not from the word.
shared.approvalRisk.unrecognised: OpsMaxx does not recognise the risk word "{{risk}}" and cannot place it on its own scale. Treat this as unscored, not as safe.
shared.approvalRisk.noConsequence: OpsMaxx cannot describe what this command does. It matched none of the shapes OpsMaxx knows, so the command itself is the only evidence there is.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.restart: Restarts {{unit}} on {{host}}. Every connection it is serving right now is dropped, and it comes back only if the unit starts cleanly — if it does not, the service stays down and nothing here starts it again.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.stop: Stops {{unit}} on {{host}} and leaves it stopped. Nothing in OpsMaxx starts it again.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.start: Starts {{unit}} on {{host}}. If it is already running this changes nothing.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.reload: Makes {{unit}} re-read its configuration on {{host}}. Existing connections are kept — but a configuration it cannot parse can still take it down.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.bootSett: Changes whether {{unit}} starts at boot on {{host}}. It does not start or stop the service right now, so the host looks unchanged until it next reboots.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.rm: Deletes files on {{host}}. There is no recycle bin over SSH — what this removes is gone.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.shutdown: Takes {{host}} down. Every SSH session, tunnel and service on it stops, and whether it comes back is up to the machine, not to OpsMaxx.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.kill: Signals running processes on {{host}}. Whatever they were part-way through is lost, and a supervised process may be restarted immediately while an unsupervised one will not be.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.packages: Changes the installed packages on {{host}}. A package manager restarts the services it touches as a side effect, so the blast radius is wider than the package named.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.firewall: Changes what {{host}} accepts network traffic on. A firewall edit made over SSH can lock this very connection out of the host, and recovering from that needs console access.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.permissi: Changes who can read, write or run those paths on {{host}}.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.accounts: Changes who can log in to {{host}}, or what they can do once they are in.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.disk: Writes to a disk or partition on {{host}} directly, underneath the filesystem. Whatever is on it is destroyed and no backup OpsMaxx knows about is taken first.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.schedule: Changes what {{host}} runs on a schedule. A scheduled job edited here runs unattended later, when nobody is watching this screen.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.containe: Stops or removes containers on {{host}}. Anything not on a named volume goes with them.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.kubectlD: Deletes objects from the Kubernetes cluster {{host}} talks to. A controller may recreate some of them and will not recreate others; kubectl does not tell you which before it runs.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.list: Lists what is in {{path}} on {{host}}. Nothing on the host changes; what the agent learns is the filenames.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.read: Reads {{path}} from {{host}} and hands the contents to the agent. Nothing on the host changes — what changes is that the contents have left it.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.overwrit: Overwrites {{path}} on {{host}}. The previous contents are not kept anywhere OpsMaxx can restore them from.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.database: Runs this statement against a database on {{host}}. OpsMaxx does not dry-run it first, and a statement that changes rows cannot be undone from here.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.serverMe: Returns {{host}}’s CPU, memory, disk and uptime — and every failed service and listening port with the process behind it, which is a service inventory of the host.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.hostFact: Returns {{host}}’s distribution, kernel and how many security updates it is waiting on. That tells the agent what this host is unpatched against.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.tunnelDe: Saves a tunnel in OpsMaxx. It does NOT start it — starting is a separate approval — but it stays in the Tunnels view afterwards, and whoever presses Start next starts what the agent wrote.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.tunnelRe: Deletes that saved tunnel. If it is running it is stopped first, and anything using it loses its connection.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.tunnelOp: Opens a tunnel between this machine and a port on {{host}}. It stays open until somebody closes it.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.tunnelCl: Closes that tunnel. Anything currently using it loses its connection.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.vpnStart: Starts a VPN profile. Your later SSH and database sessions travel over it until it is stopped.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.vpnStop: Stops a VPN profile. Sessions that reach their host through it drop.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.serverRe: Deletes this connection from OpsMaxx and its stored credential with it. OpsMaxx keeps no copy, so putting it back means typing the credential again. It does not touch the machine itself.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.serverCh: Rewrites a saved connection in OpsMaxx — where it points, which account it uses, or which saved server it jumps through. Later calls that name it, from this agent or anyone else, go wherever it now points.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.serverAd: Adds a server to OpsMaxx’s own connection list and stores a credential for it. It does not give the agent any access to the server it adds.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.viewServ: Lets the agent see that {{host}} exists and read what it is permitted to do there. No hostname, username or key is disclosed.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.ciCancel: Cancels a run on {{host}}. A pipeline stopped part-way has finished some of its steps and not the rest, and OpsMaxx cannot tell you which — a half-applied deploy is not the same as one that never ran.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.ciStart: Starts a run on {{host}}. It executes whatever that pipeline's definition says, with whatever credentials the CI server holds — OpsMaxx has not read the definition and cannot tell you what it deploys or where. Once the provider accepts the run, no agent permission can stop it: STOP ALL AI ACCESS takes away the agent's cancel along with everything else, and stopping the run is then yours to do — from this run in CI/CD, or in the provider.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.ciRead: Reads pipeline state and build output from {{host}} and hands it to the agent. Nothing on the CI server changes. The output is written by whoever opened the change that ran it, so it is text a stranger wrote arriving in the agent's context.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.fleetInv: Returns every server in {{workspace}} with its OS, pending updates and how many of them are security updates — what each host is unpatched against. It reads what OpsMaxx already collected and connects to nothing.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.fleetDri: Names every server in {{workspace}} whose watched configuration has changed since it was last reviewed. Read together, that is a list of the workspace’s weakest hosts. It reads what OpsMaxx already collected and connects to nothing.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.listAler: Returns the alerts OpsMaxx has already raised for servers in {{workspace}}. Nothing changes; it reads history already recorded.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.backupSt: Lists every backup destination configured on this machine and whether each is running on schedule — machine-wide, not only {{workspace}}. Destinations are named; their credentials are not.
shared.approvalRisk.consequence.ciConnec: Lists the names and providers of the CI/CD connections in {{workspace}}. Not their URLs or tokens, and nothing about the pipelines on them.
shared.approvalRisk.denial.workspace: Denying tells the agent this action was rejected. It stays connected and can do something else — nothing is read from {{target}}.
shared.approvalRisk.denial.server: Denying tells the agent this action was rejected. It stays connected and can do something else — nothing runs on {{server}}.
shared.jobs.outcome.orphaned: ended without recording an exit status
shared.jobs.outcome.unhealthy: restarted, and came back with something broken
shared.jobs.plan.restartsMachine: a step in this job restarts the machine
shared.jobs.detachedSettingNote: Detached jobs write one directory per step under your own state directory on each server — five small marker files, plus the job’s own output, which is as large as the command makes it — so a job survives the connection dropping. Nothing is installed and nothing runs after the job, and the directory is removed as soon as OpsMaxx has read the exit status, or swept seven days later if it never gets back. With this off, jobs run on the attached path: closing the lid mid-upgrade sends SIGHUP to the remote command, and apt and dpkg do not ignore it.
shared.cron.status.partial: only partly readable — some files were refused
shared.cron.status.denied: exists, but this account may not read it (and root was not available without a password)
shared.cron.status.noTool: nothing here can schedule a job — the tool that would read it is not installed or not running
shared.cron.status.unknown: the collector did not report on this source
shared.cron.schedule.yearly: once a year, at midnight on 1 January
shared.cron.schedule.monthly: at midnight on the 1st of each month
shared.cron.schedule.hourly: at the top of every hour
shared.cron.schedule.monthlyAt: at {{time}} on day {{day}} of each month
shared.cron.schedule.weekday.everyRange: every {{step}} days of the week from {{from}} to {{to}}
shared.cron.schedule.weekday.everyOneRan: every day of the week from {{from}} to {{to}}
shared.cron.editRefusal.systemCrontab: /etc/crontab is root-owned and is rewritten by the distribution’s own packages. OpsMaxx does not edit it: a write here needs root, and a root-owned file that a package manager also writes is not a file to round-trip from a laptop.
shared.cron.editRefusal.cronD: /etc/cron.d files are root-owned and mostly belong to packages, which replace them wholesale on upgrade. OpsMaxx does not edit them.
shared.cron.editRefusal.systemdTimer: a systemd timer is two unit files and a systemctl daemon-reload, not a line in a file. OpsMaxx reads timers and does not edit them — doing it properly is its own piece of work, and doing it improperly leaves a unit that no longer matches what systemd has loaded.
shared.cron.editRefusal.otherUserCrontab: another account’s crontab can only be written as that account or as root. OpsMaxx edits only the crontab of the account it is connected as.
shared.patch.noAutomationNote: OpsMaxx does not patch on a schedule and will not add one. It is a desktop app that gets closed, it cannot answer a dpkg conffile prompt, and it does not know what your servers do. Reporting what is pending and letting you choose is the honest version of this; for genuinely unattended patching use unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic on the server itself.
shared.patch.securityScopeNote: Security counts cover the servers whose distribution publishes them. Arch and Alpine have no security channel at all, and dnf cannot answer where the repositories omit updateinfo — those servers are excluded from the totals below rather than counted as zero.
shared.patch.command.aptSecurityRefused: apt has no single command that installs only security updates. Every recipe that claims to filters a package list and then installs its dependencies too, which is a wider change than the one you asked for. Run the full upgrade, or use unattended-upgrades on the server, which is built for exactly this.
shared.patch.command.aptDetail: apt-get update, then apt-get upgrade with the non-interactive frontend and your existing config files kept. Never dist-upgrade: nothing is removed.
shared.patch.command.dnfSecurityDetail: {{bin}} --security upgrade. On a server whose repositories publish no updateinfo this installs nothing and says so — which is why the count for such a server reads "cannot be answered" rather than 0.
shared.patch.command.dnfDetail: {{bin}} upgrade. Nothing is removed and no obsoletes are processed.
shared.patch.command.zypperSecurityDetai: zypper patch --category security. SUSE models patches as first-class objects, so this really is the security subset rather than a filtered package list.
shared.patch.command.zypperDetail: zypper update. Nothing is removed; use zypper dup by hand for a distribution jump.
shared.patch.command.pacmanSecurityRefus: Arch has no security channel, so there is no security-only upgrade to run. This is the same fact the inventory reports as "cannot be answered" for this server: it is not a permission problem and not a missing tool.
shared.patch.command.pacmanDetail: pacman -Syu. Arch is a rolling release, so this is a full system upgrade by definition — there is no smaller thing to ask for.
shared.patch.command.apkSecurityRefused: Alpine tracks security fixes per package rather than as a channel, so apk has no security-only upgrade. The inventory reports this server as "cannot be answered" for the same reason.
shared.patch.command.apkDetail: apk upgrade against the repositories already configured on the server.

shared.patch.gapHelp.probeFailed: The facts probe ran on this server and did not complete.

shared.patch.gateSamplerNote: The health data this gate reads comes from the fleet sampler — {{setting}}, under Settings → {{section}}. With that switch off nothing ever samples the estate, so no observation is ever newer than the wave and the gate can only ever time out.

shared.docker.failure.permissionDenied: This user cannot talk to the docker socket. Adding them to the docker group grants root-equivalent access on most installs, so that is a decision worth making deliberately.
shared.docker.failure.unknown: Docker returned an error that could not be classified. The raw message is below.

shared.docker.reclaim.removesVolumes_oth: removes {{count}} volumes, and what is inside a volume cannot be recovered afterwards

shared.compose.failure.notInstalled: No docker on this server. Looked on PATH and in /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, /snap/bin, /opt/homebrew/bin and /usr/sbin.
shared.compose.failure.daemonUnreachable: Docker is installed but its daemon is not answering, so it cannot say which compose projects it is running.
shared.compose.failure.permissionDenied: This user cannot talk to the docker socket, so compose cannot be asked anything. The compose FILES may still be readable — the filesystem search below does not go through the daemon.
shared.compose.failure.composeUnavailabl: Docker is here, but `docker compose` is not. That is normal on servers still running the v1 `docker-compose` script, which is a separate program with a different command line. OpsMaxx does not drive v1: its flags differ enough that guessing would be running an unverified command on someone else’s server.
shared.compose.failure.providerUnsupport: This host runs podman, and podman delegates `compose` to an external provider — here, `podman-compose`, which is a different program with a different command line. OpsMaxx does not drive it, and the reason is not tidiness: the ONE thing that keeps a compose read from printing every password in the project is `--no-interpolate --no-env-resolution`, and podman-compose rejects both flags outright. Measured on podman 5.8.4 with podman-compose 1.6.0, `podman compose config` printed a `.env` password in plaintext and there is no flag that stops it. Reading these projects here would mean choosing between an unverified command line and a credential dump.
shared.compose.failure.invalidProject: Compose read the file and refused it. The line below is compose’s own, verbatim — it names the service and the problem, and this panel has nothing to add to it.
shared.compose.failure.unknown: Compose returned an error that could not be classified. The raw message is below.
shared.compose.envDisclosure: OpsMaxx reads the NAMES of the variables in this file and never their values. The values are cut off on the server itself, so they do not cross the connection, are not held in memory here, and cannot appear in an error message. A variable is shown as set or empty; to see a value, open the file on the server.
shared.compose.refusal.down: `docker compose down` removes every container in the project, and its network with them. What it costs is not visible from a compose panel: whether a container was carrying state nobody wrote down, whether it can be recreated from the file in front of you, and whether the file in front of you is the one it was created from are three questions this UI cannot answer, and the button would be offering to act as though it had. Stop the containers instead — that is reversible, it is on the container panel already, and it is what people reach for `down` to do nine times in ten.
shared.compose.refusal.downVolumes: `docker compose down -v` deletes the project’s named volumes. That is the database. It is not recoverable, it is not undone by running `up` again, and no confirmation dialog makes it knowable from here.
shared.compose.refusal.rm: `docker compose rm` removes stopped containers. See `down`: recoverable only if you can reconstruct how they were run, which this panel cannot show you.
shared.compose.refusal.kill: `docker compose kill` sends SIGKILL with no grace period. `stop` sends SIGTERM and waits, and the difference is whether a database finishes its write.
shared.compose.lint.untagged: {{service}} has no tag on {{image}}, which means `latest`. What `up` starts tomorrow is whatever was pushed by then, and the digest on the host is not the digest in the file.
shared.compose.lint.floatingTag: {{service}} runs {{image}}. A `{{tag}}` tag moves, so `pull` then `up` can change what is running without any change to this file.
shared.compose.lint.noRestart: {{service}} has no restart policy, so compose's default of `no` applies: it does not come back after a reboot or a daemon restart.
shared.compose.lint.hostNetworkPorts: {{service}} is on the host's network and also declares {{count}} port mapping(s). Compose accepts that and ignores the mappings: the service listens on whatever port it binds inside, not on {{port}}.
shared.compose.restart.noContainer: {{service}} has no container to restart. Starting it from the file is `up`, which is on this panel already.
shared.compose.restart.tooMany: {{service}} has {{count}} containers, more than the {{max}} this acts on at once.
shared.compose.restart.fileNotApplied: This restarts the containers as they are. A change to the compose file is not applied by a restart — measured: a container whose file said one thing and whose environment said another came back with the environment it already had. `up` is what applies the file.
shared.compose.restart.allReplicas: {{service}} is {{count}} containers and all of them restart, which is what `docker compose restart {{service}}` would also do.
shared.compose.job.pullDetail: Fetches the images {{project}} declares for {{scope}}. Nothing running changes: a pulled image is used at the next `up`.
shared.compose.job.upDetail: Starts {{scope}} in {{project}} and recreates any container whose declaration has changed. Nothing is removed.

shared.compose.edit.notDeclared: `{{service}}` is not declared in this file
shared.compose.edit.builtNotPulled: `{{service}}` declares no image in this file — it is built, not pulled

shared.compose.revert.description: Put `{{service}}` back to `{{to}}`, which is what it was pinned to immediately before OpsMaxx last edited this file. It is on `{{from}}` now. This is not a guarantee that `{{to}}` was working — it is the previous line, nothing more.
shared.kubernetes.failure.notInstalled: No kubectl on this server. Looked on PATH and in /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, /snap/bin, /opt/homebrew/bin, /usr/sbin, plus the k3s, rke2 and microk8s wrappers. If it lives somewhere else, a symlink into /usr/local/bin is the usual fix.
shared.kubernetes.failure.noKubeconfig: kubectl is installed but found no kubeconfig. It looks in $KUBECONFIG then ~/.kube/config, and an SSH session may not have the same environment as a login shell.
shared.kubernetes.failure.noCluster: kubectl has a config but the cluster is not answering — the API server may be down, or the context may point somewhere unreachable from this server.
shared.kubernetes.failure.forbidden: This account is authenticated but its RBAC does not allow listing these resources. That is a different problem from there being none, and the roles it needs are named in the raw error below.
shared.kubernetes.failure.unauthorized: The cluster rejected these credentials. A token or client certificate has most likely expired.
shared.kubernetes.failure.noMetrics: kubectl top needs a Metrics API in the cluster — metrics-server, or whatever your provider ships — and nothing is answering on it. This is not "zero usage": there is no source to ask. If metrics-server was installed in the last minute or two it may simply not have scraped yet.
shared.kubernetes.failure.noPrevious: This container has no previous instance, which means it has not restarted. There is nothing to read, and that is good news about this pod rather than a failed read.
shared.kubernetes.failure.noShell: This container has no shell. That is the normal state of a distroless or scratch image and is not a broken pod — there is simply no /bin/sh inside it to run a command with, so nothing this app can send will run there. A debug sidecar (kubectl debug) is the usual way in, and it is not something this panel does.
shared.kubernetes.failure.unknown: kubectl returned an error that could not be classified. The raw message is below.

shared.dbOps.answerHelp.ok: Read successfully. A zero here means zero, not "we could not look".
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.partial: The server answered, but this account is only shown part of the picture and is not told so. Treat the numbers as a floor, never as the total.
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.denied: This exists and the account OpsMaxx connected as was not allowed to read it. A more privileged account would see more. This is NOT the same as "there is nothing here".
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.absent: The feature this question is about is not enabled on this server, so there is nothing to read.
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.notApplicable: This question does not apply to the role this server is playing.
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.unsupported: This server version cannot answer this question at all. Treat it as UNKNOWN, never as zero.
shared.dbOps.answerHelp.error: The statement failed. The server’s own words are shown beside it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.digests: Which statements read a table without using an index. Not the slow log: that counts statements which crossed a time threshold, and a statement can be fast on today’s data and still be the one that stops working when the table grows. MySQL counts the index-less executions itself, so this is its number rather than a ratio inferred from row counts — a query examining four rows to return two is scanning, and no threshold on time or rows would notice.
shared.dbOps.question.why.alwayson: Whether every replica is joined, synchronising and caught up. Zero replicas is not zero problems — a server with no availability group returns the same empty list as one whose replicas have all gone, so this reports whether AlwaysOn is configured at all before it reports health.
shared.dbOps.question.why.backups: When each database was last backed up, full and log, and whether a database in FULL recovery has ever had its log backed up. That last one is the quiet killer: the log grows until the disk fills and SQL Server does not warn anybody. Never backed up reads as never, not as long ago.
shared.dbOps.question.why.logspace: How full each transaction log is. The same failure one step later — a log nobody truncates does not slow down, it stops the database.
shared.dbOps.question.why.blocking: Sessions waiting on another session, and the one at the head of the chain. A blocked session is not slow, it is stopped, and the answer is always the head blocker rather than the queue behind it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.overview: Which server this is, what role it is playing, and how long it has been up.
shared.dbOps.question.why.replication: A replica that has stopped is a backup that is not being taken and a read pool serving stale rows. It fails silently.
shared.dbOps.question.why.archiver: A climbing failed_count is an outage in slow motion: WAL is not reaching the archive, so point-in-time recovery is already broken and pg_wal is filling the disk.
shared.dbOps.question.why.autovacuum: Transaction-ID wraparound is the one that takes a Postgres database down hard, and it announces itself for weeks first as a rising relfrozenxid age.
shared.dbOps.question.why.connections: Running out of connections refuses every new client at once, including the one you would use to fix it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.locks: One session holding a lock stalls every session behind it, and none of them look broken on their own.
shared.dbOps.question.why.sizes: Where the disk went, and which table is taking it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.statements: Which statements actually cost this server its time.
shared.dbOps.question.why.binlogs: Binary logs are point-in-time recovery and the only thing a lagging replica can catch up from. They are also a disk that fills.
shared.dbOps.question.why.slowlog: Whether the server is even recording slow queries. If it is off, the absence of slow queries means nothing.
shared.dbOps.question.why.processlist: What is running right now, and what has been running far too long.
shared.dbOps.question.why.bufferpool: A buffer pool that stopped holding the working set turns every read into disk IO.
shared.dbOps.question.why.oplog: The oplog window is how long a secondary may be down before it needs a full initial sync instead of a catch-up. It is the number that decides whether a maintenance window is safe, and it shrinks as writes speed up without anyone changing anything.
shared.dbOps.question.why.indexes: An index nothing reads is written on every insert and update to its collection and pays for itself never. The counters reset on restart, so the question is only answerable on a server that has been up a while.
shared.dbOps.question.why.currentop: What is running right now, and what has been running far too long — with the server’s own replication and journal threads excluded, because they run forever by design.
shared.dbOps.question.why.asserts: Internal assertions are the server catching itself in a state it did not expect: a corrupt index, a storage error, a bug. They are not failed client commands.
shared.dbOps.question.why.memory: An instance near its maxmemory under noeviction is a write outage waiting: Redis refuses the write rather than freeing anything, and reads carry on looking healthy while every writer fails.
shared.dbOps.question.why.persistence: Whether anything on disk would survive a restart, and how much would be lost. A failed background save leaves no current snapshot and says nothing until you need it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.clients: Running out of client slots refuses every new connection at once, including the one you would use to fix it.
shared.dbOps.question.why.keyspace: How many keys there are and how many will ever go away on their own.
shared.dbOps.question.why.stats: Two counters nothing else on this page records: connections Redis refused outright, and keys it threw away to stay under its memory limit.
shared.dbOps.question.why.cluster: A cluster that is not in state ok refuses commands for the slots it cannot serve, which from a client looks like part of the keyspace vanishing.

shared.dbOps.pg.replication.replayPaused: WAL replay is PAUSED on this standby.
It is still receiving WAL and is not applying it, so it falls further behind every second and will not be promotable.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.standbyCurre: This standby has applied every byte of WAL it has received.
pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() is NULL because no transaction has been replayed since this standby started. That is not lag — the receive and replay positions are identical.
Its last replayed transaction committed {{age}} ago, which measures how idle the PRIMARY is rather than how far behind this standby is. The receive and replay positions are identical.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.neverReplaye: This standby has not replayed a transaction yet, and its WAL positions could not be read.
pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() is NULL. That happens on a standby built moments ago and on one whose primary is idle — it is NOT a lag of zero.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.timestampOnl: This standby last replayed a transaction {{age}} ago.
The WAL byte positions could not be read, so this is a timestamp and not a lag: on an idle primary it grows while the standby is perfectly current. Treat it as a hint.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.unapplied: {{bytes}} of received WAL is not yet applied.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.standbyBehin: This standby is {{lag}} behind its primary.
shared.dbOps.pg.replication.standbyApply: This standby is applying WAL, {{bytes}} behind.

shared.dbOps.pg.archiver.off.headline: WAL archiving is off (archive_mode = {{mode}}).
shared.dbOps.pg.archiver.off.because: Nothing is being archived, so this server has no point-in-time recovery. That may be deliberate. It is reported rather than judged because OpsMaxx cannot know your recovery plan.
shared.dbOps.pg.archiver.failing.headlin: WAL archiving is FAILING — {{failures}} failure, the last {{age}} ago.
WAL archiving is FAILING — {{failures}} failures, the last {{age}} ago.
shared.dbOps.pg.archiver.failing.because: Postgres retains every WAL segment it could not archive, so pg_wal grows until the disk fills and the server stops. Nothing has ever been archived successfully from this server.
Postgres retains every WAL segment it could not archive, so pg_wal grows until the disk fills and the server stops. The last segment that did archive was {{wal}}, {{age}} ago.

shared.dbOps.pg.archiver.nothingYet.beca: No successes and no failures. On a server that has just started that is expected; on a busy one it means WAL is not being handed to the archiver.

shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.databaseWraparoun: Database {{name}} is {{pct}}% of the way to transaction-ID wraparound.
age(datfrozenxid) is {{age}} of the {{limit}} at which Postgres refuses writes. This is cluster-wide: it is not visible in this database's pg_class, and every database in the cluster stops together.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.noAges: No table ages could be read.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.tableWraparound.h: {{where}} is {{pct}}% of the way to transaction-ID wraparound.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.tableWraparound.b: age(relfrozenxid) is {{age}} of the {{limit}} at which Postgres refuses writes. Get a vacuum onto this table in a window you choose rather than one it chooses.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.forcedFreeze.head: {{where}} is {{pct}}% of the way to a forced anti-wraparound vacuum.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.forcedFreeze.beca: age(relfrozenxid) is {{age}} against an autovacuum_freeze_max_age of {{maxAge}} — {{pct}}% of the age at which Postgres refuses writes. At 100% autovacuum forces a freeze whether or not it suits you, and on a large table that is hours of IO.
shared.dbOps.pg.vacuum.approachingFreeze: {{where}} is {{pct}}% of the way to an anti-wraparound vacuum.
age(relfrozenxid) is {{age}} of {{maxAge}}. Autovacuum will force a freeze at 100%, and on a large table that is hours of IO.

shared.dbOps.pg.connections.idleInTransa: A session has been idle in transaction for {{age}}.
It holds its locks and pins the oldest snapshot, so vacuum cannot remove any row deleted since it began. This is how a table bloats without anyone writing to it.
Idle-in-transaction sessions hold back vacuum for the whole database.

shared.dbOps.mysql.channel.noErrorZeroLa: The server reported no error (Last_IO_Errno {{io}}, Last_SQL_Errno {{sql}}) — a thread that was stopped deliberately looks exactly like this. shared.dbOps.mysql.channel.lagNull.becau: Seconds_Behind_Source is NULL. MySQL returns NULL, not a number, whenever it cannot compute the lag — which in practice means replication is not running. It is NOT zero, and it is not "up to date".

shared.dbOps.mysql.bufferpool.cold.becau: {{requests}} read requests in {{uptime}} of uptime. Every first read of a cold pool is a miss, so this ratio only means something after {{minUptime}} and {{minRequests}} requests. {{size}}

shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.noMembers: This server reported no replica-set members.
replSetGetStatus answered without a members array. That is not a healthy set and it is not a standalone — a standalone raises code 76 instead.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.brokenMan: {{members}} members are not carrying the set — {{list}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.brokenEpo: The optime reported for it is the Unix epoch, which is what a member that cannot be reached reports — it is not a position and any lag computed from it is arithmetic on a placeholder.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.brokenNot: Nothing is being replicated to it, and it does not count toward a majority.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.noPrimary: This replica set has no PRIMARY.

Every member is reachable and none of them is accepting writes, so every write to this set is being refused right now. A set in this state is usually mid-election, and one that stays in it has lost its majority.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.noMajorit: Only {{healthy}} of the {{voting}} members a majority needs are healthy.
The set cannot acknowledge a majority write or elect a new primary. One more failure and it is read-only.
shared.dbOps.mongo.replication.behind.be: Reads from it return rows from that far in the past, and an election that promoted it would lose everything since.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.absent.headline: This server keeps no oplog.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.absent.because: local.oplog.rs does not exist, which is what a mongod started without --replSet looks like. There is nothing for a secondary to catch up from and nothing to measure — this is not a window of zero.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.unmeasured.head: The oplog window could not be measured.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.unmeasured.beca: The first or last oplog entry did not come back, so there is no interval to report. An unmeasured window is not a short one.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.fill: It holds {{entries}} entries in {{bytes}}, against a configured maximum of {{max}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.neverRolled.hea: The oplog covers {{window}}, which is everything since this member started {{uptime}} ago.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.neverRolled.bec: It has not yet had to discard an entry, so this is a FLOOR and not a measurement — the window will keep growing until the oplog fills for the first time. Ask again once the member has been up longer than the window you need to survive.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.short.headline: The oplog covers only {{window}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.short.because: A secondary that falls further behind than that needs a full initial sync, not a catch-up, and so does one that is stopped for maintenance for longer. The oplog is rolling: this member has been up {{uptime}} and the oldest entry is {{window}} old, so entries are being discarded.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.belowADay: Below a day is less room than most maintenance needs. This is a real measurement — the oplog is rolling, so it is not going to grow.
shared.dbOps.mongo.oplog.ok: A secondary may be down for that long and still catch up.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unreadable.he: Index usage could not be read for {{collections}} collection(s).
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unreadable.be: $indexStats was refused on {{list}}. A role with read on a database is granted $collStats and refused $indexStats on the same collection, so sizes working here is not evidence that this would.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.noCollections: There were no collections to ask about.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.countersYoung: {{unused}} of the {{droppable}} droppable indexes have not been used, but the counters are only {{age}} old.

$indexStats counts accesses since the server last started, so on a freshly restarted server every index looks unused. Nothing here can be called an unused index until the counters have been running longer than {{minAge}} — including a weekly report that only touches them on Sundays.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.allUsed: All {{droppable}} droppable indexes have been used.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.allUsedFor: All {{droppable}} droppable indexes have been used in the {{age}} the counters have been running.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unused.plain: {{unused}} of the {{droppable}} droppable indexes have had no reads.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unused.age: {{unused}} of the {{droppable}} droppable indexes have had no reads in {{age}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unused.bytes: {{unused}} of the {{droppable}} droppable indexes have had no reads, holding {{bytes}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unused.ageByt: {{unused}} of the {{droppable}} droppable indexes have had no reads in {{age}}, holding {{bytes}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.indexes.unused.becaus: {{list}}. Each one is written on every insert and update to its collection and read by nothing. Confirm against the application before dropping any of them — a counter is not a query plan, and an index that serves one nightly report reads exactly like this.
The server hit its ceiling and turned clients away. That number only ever goes up, so it may be from an incident that is over — but it did happen.
shared.dbOps.mongo.connections.noCeiling: The connection ceiling could not be read.
serverStatus does not state a maximum directly; it is current + available, and one of those did not come back. A count with no ceiling cannot be judged.
shared.dbOps.mongo.connections.nearCeili: The next client to connect will very likely be refused, including whichever one you would use to fix this.
shared.dbOps.mongo.connections.active: {{active}} of them are running an operation.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.ownOnly.hea: {{ops}} operation(s) visible, and only this connection's.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.ownOnly.bec: $currentOp was refused with allUsers: true and answered with allUsers: false. This account may not read other users’ operations, so this is only what THIS connection is doing — never treat it as the whole server.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.idle.headli: Nothing is running but the server’s own threads.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.idle.becaus: {{internal}} internal operations were excluded — the journal flusher, the checkpointer and the replication oplog tail, which is a cursor that runs for the member's entire uptime by design.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.longRunning: An operation has been running for {{age}} on {{ns}}.
shared.dbOps.mongo.currentop.noKill: {{op}}. There is no control here to kill it: see the refusal at the top of this file.
shared.dbOps.mongo.sizes.filtered.headli: {{bytes}} across {{databases}} database(s) — and that is a floor, not a total.
shared.dbOps.mongo.sizes.filtered.becaus: listDatabases came back without admin and without local, which every mongod has. The server silently answered with only the databases this account is authorized on, with ok: 1 and no warning. A more privileged account would see more.
shared.dbOps.mongo.asserts.fired.because: Regular and msg assertions are the server catching itself in a state it did not expect — a corrupt index, a storage-engine error, a bug. They are not failed client commands; those are counted separately as user assertions and are normal.
shared.dbOps.mongo.asserts.rolledOver.he: The assertion counters have rolled over {{rollovers}} time(s).
shared.dbOps.mongo.asserts.rolledOver.be: They roll at 2^30, so the numbers beside them have restarted from zero and the totals below are not totals.
shared.dbOps.mongo.asserts.pageFaultsUnr: Page faults are not reported on this platform — serverStatus says so itself, in extra_info.note, and that is different from a count of zero.
shared.dbOps.mongo.asserts.userNormal: User assertions are failed client commands — a duplicate key, a bad query — and a healthy server has plenty.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.noLimitReporte: Using {{used}}, against a limit this server did not report.

There was no maxmemory line in INFO memory at all. That is NOT the same as maxmemory being zero — an absent field means this build or version does not say, and the usage above cannot be judged against anything.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.unlimited.head: Using {{used}} with NO memory limit set.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.unlimited.beca: maxmemory is 0, which Redis means as unlimited — this is a real answer and not a missing one. Nothing stops this instance growing until the machine runs out and the kernel picks a process to kill, and the kernel usually picks the largest one. On a replica of a bounded master it may be deliberate; on a master it is the outage that has not happened yet.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.unmeasured.hea: Memory usage could not be measured.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.unmeasured.bec: used_memory did not come back, so there is nothing to compare with the limit.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.noEvictionFull: With noeviction, Redis does not free anything to make room — it refuses the write. At this fill level the next write that needs memory comes back as OOM command not allowed, and every writing client fails at once while reads carry on looking healthy.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.overLimit: It is over its own limit. Redis permits this when a single command allocates past the line, which is why the number can exceed 100%.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.evicting: Keys are being evicted under {{policy}} to stay under the limit, so data is being dropped to make room.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.noEvictionNear: With noeviction, reaching the limit refuses writes rather than freeing anything.
shared.dbOps.redis.memory.fragmentation: Fragmentation ratio {{ratio}}: the process holds that much more from the OS than it is using.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.loading.h: This instance is still loading its dataset.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.loading.b: Nothing else on this page is a steady-state measurement until it has finished.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.rdbFailed: There is no current snapshot on disk. A restart from here loses everything written since the last save that did work, and the usual cause is that the fork could not get memory.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.aofFailed: The append-only file is not being written (aof_last_write_status: {{status}}).
AOF is on and the last write to it failed, so the durability this instance is configured for is not happening. Usually a full disk.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.unreadabl: Persistence state could not be read.
Neither an AOF nor an RDB save time came back.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.rdbOnly: AOF is off; the last RDB save was {{age}} ago with {{changes}} changes since.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.rdbStaleA: Everything written in that window exists only in memory. A restart, an OOM kill or a crash loses all of it.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.rdbStaleW: That is how much data a restart would lose.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.rewriteFa: The file is still being written, so nothing is lost yet, but it is not being compacted and it will keep growing.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.aofOn: AOF is on and its last write was {{status}}.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.aofOnUnre: AOF is on and its last write was not reported.
shared.dbOps.redis.persistence.lastRdbSa: The last RDB save was {{age}} ago.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.lostMaste: This replica has LOST its master (master_link_status: {{status}}).
This replica has LOST its master, {{age}} ago (master_link_status: {{status}}).
It is serving whatever it had when the link dropped, and every write since then is missing.

It is serving whatever it had when the link dropped, and every write since then is missing. Redis reports master_last_io_seconds_ago as -1 here, which is its way of saying it has no measurement at all — it is not "zero seconds ago".
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.resyncing: This replica is mid-resynchronisation with its master.
Its dataset is incomplete until the sync finishes, so reads from it are not trustworthy yet.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.replicati: Replicating from {{master}}, last heard from {{age}} ago.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.silentLin: A link that is nominally up and silent for that long is a link that is about to be declared down.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.atOffset: At offset {{offset}}. Whether that is level with the master cannot be told from here — this instance only reports its own offset.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.roleUnrea: The replication role could not be read.
INFO replication did not report connected_slaves.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.noReplica: This is a master with no replicas connected.

Whether that is correct cannot be answered from INFO. A standalone Redis reports exactly this line and is completely healthy; so does a master whose only replica died a minute ago, and the two are identical strings. OpsMaxx does not read a Sentinel or a cluster configuration, so it does not know which this is — and calling it healthy would be a guess in the hour it matters.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.offline.b: A replica in any state other than online is not receiving the stream, whatever its offset says.
shared.dbOps.redis.replication.furthestB: Furthest behind by {{bytes}} of replication stream.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.noThreshold.h: {{entries}} entries in the slow log, recorded above a threshold this account could not read.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.noThreshold.b: Without slowlog-log-slower-than the log cannot be interpreted: an empty log means "nothing was slow" at 10 ms and means nothing at all at 10 seconds.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.off.headline: The slow log is switched OFF (slowlog-log-slower-than is negative).
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.off.because: Nothing is being recorded, so the log being empty says nothing about whether this server has slow commands. Redis has no other record of them.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.everything.he: The slow log records EVERY command (slowlog-log-slower-than is 0).
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.everything.be: A log of everything cannot tell you what is slow, and it costs memory and time on every command. It also fills with this panel’s own reads: the entries below will largely be the INFO calls that produced this page.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.rolled: The log is at its maximum of {{max}} entries, so older ones have already been discarded.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.empty: Nothing has taken longer than {{threshold}} ms since the log was last reset.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.slowest: Slowest recorded command: {{command}} at {{ms}} ms, against a {{threshold}} ms threshold.
shared.dbOps.redis.slowlog.blockedEveryo: Redis runs commands one at a time, so every other client on this instance waited for that. {{held}}
shared.dbOps.redis.clients.blocked: {{blocked}} of them are blocked on a command like BLPOP, which is normal for a queue consumer and not a stall.
shared.dbOps.redis.clients.noCeiling.hea: {{connected}} clients connected, against a ceiling this server did not report.
shared.dbOps.redis.clients.noCeiling.bec: INFO clients has no maxclients line at all here — Redis did not add it until 6.0, and this is the field the whole question compares against. An absent ceiling is not an unlimited one and it is not zero.
shared.dbOps.redis.clients.unreadable.he: The client count could not be read.
shared.dbOps.redis.clients.atCeiling: At the ceiling Redis refuses new connections outright, and the refusals are counted in INFO stats as rejected_connections.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.unreadable.h: The keyspace could not be read.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.unreadable.b: INFO keyspace did not come back at all.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.empty.becaus: INFO keyspace omits a database entirely when it is empty, so a bare section here genuinely does mean zero — unlike an absent field anywhere else on this page.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.summary: {{keys}} keys across {{databases}} database(s), {{expiring}} of them with an expiry.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.noTtl: {{keys}} keys have no TTL and the policy is noeviction, so nothing will ever remove them. That combination is what takes an instance to its memory limit and then refuses every write.
shared.dbOps.redis.keyspace.selectedDb: The database this connection is pointed at holds {{keys}}.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.refused.headlin: {{refused}} connections have been REFUSED because maxclients was reached.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.refused.because: Every one of those was a client that could not talk to Redis at all. The counter only rises, so it may be from an incident that has passed — but it did happen, and nothing else on this page records it.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.evicted.headlin: {{evicted}} keys have been evicted to stay under the memory limit.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.evicted.because: Data that was written was thrown away to make room. For a cache that is the design; for anything treated as a store it is silent data loss.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.unreported.head: Neither the rejected-connection nor the eviction counter was reported.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.unreported.beca: INFO stats did not carry them, so nothing here can be said about either.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.ok: No connections refused and no keys evicted.
shared.dbOps.redis.stats.expired: {{expired}} keys have expired normally, which is not eviction.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.unreadable.he: Whether this instance is in a cluster could not be read.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.unreadable.be: INFO cluster did not report cluster_enabled.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.off.headline: Cluster mode is off.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.off.because: CLUSTER INFO on this instance answers "ERR This instance has cluster support disabled", which is a fact rather than a failure. Nothing about slots or cluster state applies.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.state.because: While the state is not ok the cluster refuses commands for the slots it cannot serve, which from a client looks like part of the keyspace disappearing.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.slots.headlin: Only {{assigned}} of 16384 hash slots are assigned.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.slots.because: Every key that hashes into an unassigned slot is unreachable. The cluster is incomplete, whatever cluster_state says.
shared.dbOps.redis.cluster.ok.headline: Cluster state ok across {{nodes}} known nodes.

shared.k8sAllocatable.noSchedulable: Every node is cordoned or could not be sized, so there is no schedulable capacity to report.
